    [A column of work-incipits follows—the opening words of listed works—partly illegible: "By what bond the heart is held…"; "It arises from violent operation…"; "Blessed the man who knows [his] infirmity…"; "There are three orders in which…"; "A man of much solicitude…"; "The virtues succeed one another…"; "This is the order, sober and to God…"; "The fortitude which they set…"; "Formulas of spiritual understanding…"; "Your love demands…"; "Of the Roman Church, to which God…"]

    Book

    Proba, a most elegant woman, wife of Adelphus, Roman proconsul; a woman most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures; burning with remarkable zeal, she surpassed her sex by her learning. Perfectly trained in Greek and Latin letters, and excelling in verse and prose, since she held Virgil in her mind word for word, she conceived the idea of describing the New and Old Testament from his verses, as though he had intended to show this meaning in his poems. And so, vigorously undertaking the work stored up in her mind, carefully going through all the books of Virgil, taking now this, now that verse, sometimes a half-verse, and at times smaller parts of verses, with remarkable industry and everywhere preserving the measure of the feet, she described the catholic volumes in the poet’s verses; and she entitled this work, in almost seven hundred verses, with a Greek word:

    A Virgilian cento, one book.

    Whether she wrote anything more, I do not know. Nevertheless this work is counted among the apocrypha, because even if a devout woman undertook a pious study, still Virgil never judged that his little verses should be referred to the honor of Christ or to our faith. For the interpretation of this matter is not Virgil’s own, but a fictive one assumed by Proba. She flourished, as some think, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

    Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, a woman most devoted in the Christian religion and most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters: returning from Jerusalem, she brought with her the relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen, and honorably placed them in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Since she was very learned, excelling in verse and prose, she is said, in imitation of Proba, wife of Adelphus, to have turned the poems of Homer back to the Christian faith, likewise prefixing to the little published work this title:

    Homeric centos, one book.

    But this too is apocryphal. She also wrote certain other things. Since Saint Jerome says in a certain letter that he had read Homeric centos and Virgilian centos, they must necessarily have been composed before his death. She flourished with her husband Theodosius, who took up the empire in the year of the Lord 423.

    Primasius, an African bishop, and, as some hold, once a disciple of blessed Augustine, a man indeed learned in the holy Scriptures, excellently trained in the disciplines, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, is said to have composed many little works, which among the ancients were held in great esteem. Of these I have found only:

    Against Heresies, to Bishop Fortunatus, three books.

    On the Apocalypse of John, to Castorius, five books. On the book of the Apocalypse of blessed John, to [unclear].

    The other things that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Theodosius II, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Eunilius, bishop of a certain city in Africa, [unclear], certainly a man very learned in the sacred Scriptures, in my judgment sufficiently trained in secular discipline, profound in understanding, sweet and ornate in speech, is said to have compiled many little works; but I have seen only the distinguished work that he wrote to the above-named Bishop Primasius, which he entitled:

    On the Parts of the Divine Law, one book. To the holy and most blessed Bishop Pri[masius].

    Of the rest I have seen none. He flourished at the same time as Primasius, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Roterius, bishop of Alexandria, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, an outstanding theologian and computist; in the times of the emperor Leo, after a sedition had been stirred up, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus cruelly killed him as an instigator on behalf of Timothy, and they set up that same Timothy in his place, as an idol for the Alexandrian bishop. Among other things he wrote to Saint Pope Leo.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 29

    On the celebration of Easter: 3 epistles. To Hilary on the same matter: an epistle. Several letters to various persons. And certain other works. “Since your holiness arose.” He flourished under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

    Paschasinus, a Sicilian bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, worthy of reverence no less for his conduct than for his knowledge, is said to have presided in place of the blessed Pope Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, in which, together with the holy fathers, numbering two hundred, he condemned the heretics Eutyches and Dioscorus. Eutyches was a priest and abbot of the very celebrated monastery of Constantinople, who asserted that Christ was only God and not man; and he wrote various works on behalf of his error, all of which were condemned together with their author. Paschasinus, however, wrote to Pope Leo:

    On the question of Easter: an epistle. To the same, on the miracle of the font: an epistle. The acts of the Council of Chalcedon: a book. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 450.

    Leo, the first pope, by birth a Tuscan, after Sixtus III sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in delivering homilies to the people so celebrated and eloquent that he had no superior in the Roman Church, as his very famous sermons testify. For he was the Cicero of ecclesiastical speech, the Homer of sacred theology, the Aristotle of the arguments of faith, the Peter of apostolic authority, and Paul in the Christian pulpit. His sermons penetrate the heart, move the mind, and confirm the Catholic faith with sweet brevity of speech. Nor is this surprising: bearing the fire of divine love kindled in his breast, what else could he speak but burning words? He wrote many short works. Of these I have found only the following, namely:

    Against Eutyches the priest: a book. On the Nicene Creed: a book. To Emperor Leo, of testimonies: a book. To the inquiries of Bishop Januarius: a book. On the Passion of the Lord: 24 homilies, a book. Many homilies to the people: a book. To Flavianus the bishop, against Eutyches: a book. To Emperor Leo, against Eutyches: a book. To Bishop Turibius, against the Priscillianists: a book. To Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne: a book. To Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica: a book. Many letters to various persons: a book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

    At length he died, after many labors for the benefit of the Church, under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 461, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

    Peter, bishop of Ravenna, a learned and very holy man, shining in life with many miracles, was of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people, and converted many to the path of truth as much by word as by example. He wrote many things for the edification of the faithful. Of these there are circulated:

    Several sermons and homilies: epistles. To Eutyches the priest: an epistle. He also wrote several other letters. He flourished under Emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

    Flavianus, bishop of Constantinople, to whom blessed Pope Leo wrote many letters, a man indeed learned and a notable lover of Catholic unity, [unclear] Eutyches the priest and archimandrite, who held impious opinions concerning the humanity of Christ,

    ... he deposed and excommunicated, as is attested in a certain letter sent to the aforesaid Pope Leo; he did and endured many things for the extirpation of heresies. He wrote in the Greek language certain works not to be despised, of which the following are reported:

    Acts with Eutyches the presbyter, one book. Against the errors of the same, one book. To Pope Leo on the same matter, a letter: “No thing [unclear] the poisons of the devil.” Letters to various persons, one book. And some other things which we do not know.

    He flourished under Theodosius the Younger and Marcian, in the year of the Lord 454.

    Hilarius, pope, by nation a Sardinian, after Leo the Great sat in the pontificate for six years and as many months; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished by the adornment of many virtues, who, constantly intent upon alms and holy works, shone with no small reputation for sanctity. He, after holding a synod of fifty bishops at Rome, established certain things for ecclesiastical honor. He wrote certain necessary little works; of these I have found only:

    A synodal decree, one book: “Since the religious [unclear].” To the bishops of the province of Tarragona, a letter: “After your letters.” To Ascanius, bishop of Tarragona, a letter: “Of the divine grace toward us.” On the Council of Nicaea, one letter. On the Council of Ephesus, one letter. On the Council of Chalcedon, one letter. Letters to various persons, one book.

    He died under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 468, in the sixth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March; Simplicius succeeded him.

    Eusebius, bishop of Milan, learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, beloved and intimate with the most blessed pontiff Leo, fought bravely for the holy catholic faith against the heretics by writing. He is said to have published some little works for the edification of the faithful, but they have not come to my knowledge.

    For I have seen only one letter of his, which he is said to have written in matters of faith:

    To Saint Pope Leo, a letter: “The brethren having returned, with the Lord granting it.”

    He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 401.

    Asclepius the African, bishop of the territory of Vaga, a studious and learned man, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, a most vigorous assailant of heretics, wrote many volumes for the edification of the people; by the publication of these he was named glorious in every land, since he showed himself a useful teacher to the common people not only in words but also in works. For in his age many very learned men made it renowned. Of his writings the following are reported:

    Against the Donatists, one book. Against the Arians, one book. Countless homilies to the people, one book. And many other things unknown to us.

    He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

    Prosper, bishop of Reggio, an Aquitanian after Faventius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, eloquent in speech, profound in understanding, subtle in talent, vigorous in assertion, appeared most holy in life and conduct. He was once notary of blessed Pope Leo the Great and dictated many letters in his person. He also wrote from his own vein many excellent little works. Of these I have found only the items set down below. From the Sentences of blessed Augustine, bishop, in hexameter and pentameter verses, mixed with prose, a very beautiful work which he wished to preface:

    Epigrams, one book: “While it pleases the mind with sacred things.”

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 30

    On the contemplative life: three books. “The contemplative life, in which...” On free will: one book. “To the lord brother, most beloved, Rusi...” Responses to the chapters of the Gauls: one book. “The doctrine which of holy me...” To the objections of the Vincentians: one book. “Certain men of Christian and fra...” To the excerpts of the Genoese: one book. “In the books of blessed memory...” A great Summa of 330 propositions: one book. “True knowledge is that which neither...” Against Cassian on free will: one book. A chronicle of histories: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. On illustrious men: one book. On the captivity of Rome: one book. He is said besides to have written some other works, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the time of Leo the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 460. His feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

    lector

    [Unclear] an excellent declaimer of sermons, and a notable persecutor of heretics, is said to have compiled many volumes, in which he instructed the devout people and strongly refuted those erring concerning the faith. Among these the following are reported:

    Against the Arians: one book. Against the Donatists: one book. A consolatory work to Basilius: one book. On penance also: one book. Homilies to the people: two books. He also published not a few other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 550.

    ectorinus

    Victorinus, an Aquitanian by nation, a man very devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, is said to have left certain little works of his own talent, which have as yet by no means come to my knowledge. At the command of Pope Hilarius he wrote, for finding the term of Easter:

    The great cycle of 532 years: one book.

    This is called the great cycle of 532 years; when these have passed, all computations of the luminaries return to the same point. Dionysius the abbot afterward corrected it, and down to this our age, although it has failed in some respects, nevertheless it has endured. This Victorinus also wrote certain letters. He flourished under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460, and wrote his cycle under Pope Hilarius, in the third year of his pontificate.

    p

    Petrus, presbyter of the church of Edessa, practiced in the holy Scriptures, and endowed with a most excellent natural ability for declaiming homilies to the people, so that in his own times he had no equal. He wrote in the Syriac language many distinguished volumes, of which only very few titles have come to my knowledge:

    Commentaries on the Psalms: one book. He also played with the Psalms in meter: one book.

    He dictated and delivered homilies to the people, almost infinitely many, which are rarely found among us. But neither is the number of his treatises certain to us. He flourished under Emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

    Abatius

    Abatius, bishop of the Gallican province, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle and keen in intellect, often fought against the madness of heretics, both by writing and by disputing. Hence, having been asked by a certain Secunda, a virgin dedicated to Christ, he wrote a distinguished and memorable volume:

    Against Marcion and Valentinus: one book. Against Eunomius and Aetius: one book. He also published some other works, but they have not yet come to my knowledge.

    Book C

    [Ursinus?] the monk, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of humane letters, subtle in intellect, cautious in speech, is said to have composed many treatises for the benefit of the faithful; but I do not recall that anything of his has ever come into our hands. There is, however, reported an outstanding work of his against those who rebaptize persons once duly baptized, whose title is:

    On the manner of not rebaptizing heretics, one book.

    He flourished, as I find, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

    Julianus, bishop of the church of Toledo in Spain, and by nation a Moor, to whom Saint Prosper is said to have written three books On Contemplation, was a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular disciplines, scholastic in speech, apt in understanding. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported:

    The faith of the nascent Church, by testimonies, [unclear]. On holy virginity, one book. On the nature of the soul, eight books. On the resurrection, questions, one book. On contempt of the world, one book. Prognosticon of the future age, two books. On vices and virtues, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

    He is also said to have composed some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

    He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 550.

    Victorinus Buconius, bishop of the city of [Castellum?] in Mauritania, a man exercised by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned in secular letters and disciplines, a very strong hammer against heretics and an outstanding teacher of the faithful people, is said to have written many little works for the defense of the catholic faith. Of these the principal ones are reported to be these:

    Against the Jews, one book. Against the Arians, one book. Against all heretics, two books. On the sacraments also, one book.

    He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

    Musaeus, priest of the church of Marseilles, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and polished by very subtle exercise in their meanings, scholastic and refined in language, at the urging of Saint Venerius the bishop, extracted from the sacred Scriptures responsive readings suited to each feast day throughout the whole year, and arranged psalms suited to the several times to be sung in church. He also wrote to Bishop Eustasius an outstanding work:

    Of sacraments, seven books. Several homilies to the people. And certain other things.

    He flourished under the princes Marcian and Leo, in the year of the Lord 440.

    Vincentius, a priest, by nation a Gaul, much exercised in the divine Scriptures, having a language polished by practice in speaking and by great reading, and also not ignorant of secular letters, wrote, as our Gennadius reports, an outstanding work, and one to be embraced most greatly by devout men:

    Commentaries on the Psalms, one book. And certain other things.

    He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

    Cyrus, Alexandrian by birth, a physician by profession, from a philosopher made a monk for the love of Christ, a man most learned in secular letters, distinguished in skill of speaking, using syllogisms in his writings more than the authorities of divine readings: while he inveighs too strongly against Nestorius, he seems to foster the Timothean doctrine, and, uncertain, he suspends his mind from assent to the Council of Chalcedon, nor does he think it should be accepted that the Son of God after the incarnation consists of two natures. Of his writings there is reported:

    Against Nestorius, one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers Folio 31

    Against the heretics: one book.

    He flourished under Emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

    Salvianus, presbyter of the church of Marseille, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, a teacher of the bishops of his time, wrote in a scholastic and clear style many and various little works, of which the following are reported. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, he wrote several letters seasoned with the salt of wisdom. To Marcellus the presbyter:

    On the good of virginity: three books. Against avarice: four books. On the present judgment: five books. To Bishop Salonius: one book. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne: one book. On the beginning of Genesis, the Hexaemeron: one book. On the final part of Ecclesiastes: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Homilies made to bishops: one book. Also On the Sacraments: one book. Many homilies to the people: one book. He also published many other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

    He flourished under Emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Emanuel, presbyter of the church of Edessa, learned in the divine Scriptures through continual exercise, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, skilled in Greek and Syriac speech, flourished first at Edessa; afterward, coming to Constantinople, and being held there in great esteem, he ended his last day. He wrote, both in Greek and in Syriac, almost innumerable little works. Of these, very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only:

    Against the Nestorians: one book. Against the Eutychians: one book. Against the Timotheans: one book.

    He flourished under Emperor Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Gennadius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in Greek some little works on the sacred volumes, but they have by no means come into our hands. For he was an outstanding declaimer of homilies, and distinguished no less in life than in knowledge of the Scriptures. Among other things, a work of his arranged as commentaries is reported:

    On Daniel the prophet: one book. Many homilies to the people: one book.

    He died under Emperor Leo I, who was reigning in the year of the Lord 460.

    Claudius, bishop of Vienne, to whom the presbyter Salvianus composed one book, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters; no less distinguished in holiness than in knowledge, he shone forth in his own times. Because of frequent earthquakes, he first instituted the litanies, which the Roman Church thereafter took up and continued. He wrote:

    On the state of the soul: three books. Also Letters: one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    And let the name Claudius not trouble the uninformed: he should know that the same man is called Mamertus.

    Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the judgment of all, the most learned man of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, many distinguished little works. Of these I was able to find only those which I have set down below, namely:

    A panegyric to Anthemius Augustus: one book. A panegyric to Julius Valerius: one book. By auspice and number [unclear]. Conceive the past things.

    Book

    A panegyric to his father-in-law: 1 book, beginning “Phoebus, having at last traversed [unclear].” To Felix: 1 book, beginning “Speak, speak, what I ask, great one.” An epithalamium for Ruricius and Hiberia: 1 book, beginning “Among the dark-blue [unclear].” An epithalamium for Polemius: 1 book, beginning “By chance, returning [unclear].” Eucharisticon to Faustus: 1 book, beginning “Phoebus and three times three.” Of epigrams also: 1 book, beginning “Four days before.” To Pontius Leontius of Burgus: 1 book, beginning “The stable of the Bistonian king.” In praise of the city of Narbonne: 1 book, beginning “Hail, mighty Narbonne.” Letters to various persons: 9 books, beginning “Long ago, most excellent lord, greater [unclear].”

    He also wrote many other compositions, short indeed but sufficiently learned, whose titles I have passed over for love of brevity. He flourished in the time of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Simplicius, pope, by birth a Tiburtine, after the death of Hilarius presided over the Roman and universal Church for fifteen years. He was a learned and holy man, who appeared not only simple according to his name, but also upright, turning away from evil and fearing God. He restored many churches that had collapsed from extreme age; he issued statutes necessary for the Christian commonwealth; and he wrote some things for the edification of the faithful. Of these I have read only:

    To John, bishop of Ravenna: 1 letter, beginning “If anyone, contemplating the Church [unclear].” To Florentius and Equitius, bishops: 1 letter, beginning “The report of your belovedness [unclear].” To Severus, bishop: 1 letter.

    But he also wrote many other very useful letters, which I have not yet seen. He died under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 483, in the sixth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, and was carried to [unclear].

    Eruuldeus, bishop of a certain church: I have not been able to find the name of the city. He was a man learned by constant practice in the divine Scriptures, rich in reading of the ancients, subtle in intellect, apt in speech. He is said to have produced some little works. Of these there survives a volume, furnished from the sacred Scriptures, against those who say that Christ, while dwelling in this life, did not see the Father with his fleshly eyes. The heading of this work is:

    That the Son saw the Father: 1 book.

    He also wrote certain other things.

    In this work he shows that the Son of God, even from the hour of his conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, always saw his God and Father with fleshly eyes, both thereafter and now, clothed in human flesh. He is said to have flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Victor, bishop of Capua, learned in the sacred Scriptures and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, an excellent theologian and computist, keen in intellect and distinguished in speech, is said to have written some little works on the sacred volumes; but very few of them have come to my knowledge. He refuted the error of Victorius of Aquitaine, who, at the command of Pope Hilarius, writing paschal cycles, taught that Easter should be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May in the year of the Lord 455, although it was more correctly to be celebrated in that year on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Therefore, when this occasion arose, he wrote:

    On Easter. One Gospel from the four: 1 book.

    He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Erealis, an African bishop, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of the discipline of secular studies. When he was asked by Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, whether he could assign in a few words testimonies of divine Scripture, without disputations, merely for the assertion of the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, he answered not in a few words, as that man had mockingly requested, but by composing a distinguished work with many testimonies from both Testaments:

    Against the Arians.

    He also wrote other things. He flourished in the time of the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

    John, priest of the church of Antioch, rich in reading of the ancients in the sacred Scriptures. When he had taught grammar at Antioch for some years, he began to wish to profess himself a cleric; and, having become a priest by legitimate succession [unclear], he [unclear] himself to divine readings

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 32

    ... produced; having been made more learned by them, he was so powerful in delivering homilies that he had no one like him in his own time. He wrote a sufficiently well-furnished volume:

    Against the Timotheans: one book. Several homilies to the people: one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Theodolus, a priest, Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, coming from Italy into Coelesyria, is remembered there as having been ordained priest and finally bishop; and by writing and composing many things he transmitted his name to posterity. Of his little works I have found only a metrical work on the miracles of the Old Testament and the fables of the poets, to which he gave the title:

    Eclogues: one book. On the harmony of the Scriptures: one book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the year of the Lord 480 under the emperor Zeno, under whom he also died.

    Eugenius, bishop of Carthage in Africa, a learned and holy man, a public confessor of the undivided Trinity, endured many injuries from the Arians under Huneric, king of the Vandals, who after Genseric his father persecuted Christians in Africa. For with many other bishops, after their tongues had been cut out, he was sent into exile. He wrote, moreover, certain little works full of faith and learning, of which the following are reported:

    Exposition of the Catholic Faith: one book. A disputation held with the Arians: one book. An apologetic for the faith: one book. To his church, while he was going into exile: a letter. He is nevertheless said to have written other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

    Felix, the third pope, Roman by nation, after Saint Simplicius the pontiff sat in the chair of Peter for eight years; a good, learned, and holy man, who, kindled with zeal for the faith, condemned Peter and Acacius, Eutychian bishops, and banished them into exile. For this reason, holding a synod at Rome, he established many things for ecclesiastical utility, and wrote:

    A synodal decree: one book. Several decretal letters: one book. He died under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 493, in the first indiction.

    Gennadius, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, perfectly instructed in both Greek and Latin eloquence, composed many little works, and translated not a few volumes of the ancient fathers from Greek into the Latin tongue. Concerning his own writings he himself, at the end of Illustrious Men, listed the following:

    On his faith, to Pope Gelasius: one book. Against Nestorius: six books. Against Eutyches: eleven books. Against Pelagius: three books. Against all heresies: eight books. On illustrious men: one book. Jacobus, surnamed the Wise. On the heresy of the thousand years: one book. He wrote these and certain other things, but they have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

    Gelasius, the first pope, African by nation, sat after Felix in the pontificate for four years; a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures. Soon after entering upon the pontifical office, he sent into exile the Manichaeans whom he found in the city, and publicly burned their books at the basilica of Saint Mary Major. He established many things for ecclesiastical utility, and wrote very many things against heretics. Of his little works the following are reported:

    Book

    A synodal decree: one book. “The arrangement of necessary matters...” Against the Arians: three books. Against Eutyches and Nestorius: five books. Hymns in the manner of Ambrose: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Several weighty orations. And certain other works. He arranged Graduals, Alleluias, and Tracts, with prefaces suitable for the Mass; he separated the authentic books of the holy fathers from the apocryphal, as is found in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. He died while Anastasius Augustus was emperor, in the year of the Lord 496.

    Faustus, from being abbot of the monastery of Lerins, became bishop of Riez in Gaul: a learned and eloquent man, indeed, but stained by the Pelagian error. For this reason his little works are counted among the apocrypha, as is clear in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. At length, corrected and amended by blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, he abandoned the error and returned to the truth of the catholic faith; as proof of this he published an excellent work against his former errors, which he entitled On the Grace of God. Of his small works they report the following. The same volume:

    On the grace of God: one book. “The catholic faith in the universe...” Against the Arians: one book. Against the Anthropomorphites: one book. On the Holy Spirit: one book. To Gratus the deacon, against Nestorius: one book. To Felix the prefect: one book. Several homilies to the people. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year 490.

    Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, was a man most learned in the divine scriptures and nobly trained in secular letters; subtle in ability, profound in understanding, sweet in speech, polished in expression, easy in teaching, sharp in argument, fit for persuasion, and very gentle. He shone forth no less clearly for holiness of life than for knowledge of the scriptures. He wrote many outstanding volumes, of which the following are reported:

    On the grace of God and free will: seven books. “Your letter, dearest son...” On the Holy Trinity: one book. “Your letter, holy brother, [unclear]...” On the truth of predestination: three books. “Your letter, with holy concern...” On the remission of sins: three books. “With spiritual desire and...” A disputation with King Thrasamund: one book. “To the lady most greatly in Christ...” The rule of true life: one book. “Would that, holy brother, so great...” To Ferrandus the deacon: one book. “Just as the true light in no way...” On marital continence: one book. “That, unknown in body, [unclear]...” On virginity, to Proba: one book. “Some months ago, the deacon...” On prayer, to the same: one book. On charity, to Abbot Eugippius: one book. On penance, to Venantia: one book. To the senator Theodore: one book. To Galla the widow: one book. On faith, to Donatus: one book. On the mystery of the mediator: one book. On the sacrament of the incarnation: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Of many sermons: one book. Innumerable homilies also: one book. On various questions: one book. On Adam without Abel, or without [unclear]: three books. “Although he seeks an ineffective...” Mythologies, to Catus the priest: one book. “Lest concerning your teachers...” On obscure expressions: one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 33

    The moralities of the Virgilian contents, a book. On the immensity of the Son of God, a book. On the Passion of the Lord, a book.

    But he is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was splendidly trained in both Greek and Latin speech. It should be noted, however, that the title of the book on Adam without A is The Book without Letters; namely, on Abel without B, on Cain without C, and so on with the rest according to the sequence of the letters. But in the book whose title is Exposition of the Virgilian Contents according to the Moral Philosophers, with wonderful industry he sought gold in mud, so to speak, and found it, when he inclined the poet’s work toward natural-philosophical reasoning. He wrote this work to a certain deacon. Another work, of mythologies, he wrote to Catus, a Carthaginian priest; and On the Obscure Expressions of the Ancients to Chalcidius the grammarian, already an old man, when he himself was still young, and teacher and rector of a school of humane letters. He flourished in the times of Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, persecutor of the Catholic churches, under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

    Ferrandus, deacon of the church of Carthage, to whom there survive some little works of the above-mentioned Saint Fulgentius, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and venerable no less for the holiness of his way of life than for his learning. He is reported to have brought forth certain volumes of lively intelligence, of which only the following have come to my knowledge:

    To Count Reginus, On the Seven Rules of Innocence, one book: “From the labors of social life.” To Saint Fulgentius, one letter. A book of letters to various persons. He flourished with Fulgentius, under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

    Anastasius II, pope, Roman by nation, sat after the holy pontiff Gelasius for one year and ten months. He was indeed a learned man, but, led astray by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, he not long afterward paid the due penalties for his error. For when he wished to obey the necessity of nature, struck by God, the wretched man poured out his entrails with torches, as is clear in distinction 19, Anastasius. And this was the second infamous pope. He wrote to the emperor Anastasius:

    On the Peace of the Church, one letter: “The beginning of my pontificate.” He is also said to have written other letters, but they have not come into our hands. He died, struck by divine judgment, when he had secretly wished to recall from exile Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and cast out by the Church, under Anastasius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 498.

    Paschasius, deacon of the Roman church, a learned and holy man, father of the poor, wholly intent upon the giving of alms, was of such virtue and holiness that Pope Gregory writes in the fourth book of the Dialogues that a demoniac was healed after his death by the touch of his dalmatic. Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, saw his soul in the punishments of purgatory, tormented for nothing other than that in the election of Pope Symmachus he had himself rather chosen Laurence, and in this opinion, though with peace, had persevered until death. On Gregory’s testimony he wrote a distinguished volume:

    On the Holy Spirit, three books, against the errors of the Greeks. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

    Symmachus, pope, Sardinian by nation, a learned and holy man, obtained the pontificate after Anastasius, not without discord between the parties of Laurence, and sat for fifteen years and six months. A man merciful and generous to the poor, he loved the clergy, enriched the churches, and drove the heretics from the city. Having held a synod at Rome of 120 bishops concerning the crimes charged against him, he cleared himself canonically, and drove Peter, bishop of Ravenna, with his accomplices into exile. He wrote certain letters and little works not to be despised. Of these I have found:

    Decree of the first synod, one book: “On account of the frequent ambitions.” Decree of the Roman synod, one book: “When in one place at blessed Peter’s.” Acts of another Roman synod, one book: “The fourth synod held at Rome.” On the excesses of clerics, one book: “Your fraternity indeed well.” A book of letters to various persons.

    BOOK

    He died under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 515, in the eighth indiction, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. Pope Hormisdas succeeded him.

    Symmachus, patrician, senator, and Roman consul, father-in-law of Boethius, a philosopher and distinguished orator, and a magnificent worshipper of the Christian faith, whom Theodoric, king of Italy, because of suspicion that he had aimed at liberty, banished into exile together with Boethius at Pavia, and not long afterward cruelly slew. Since he was a learned and most eloquent man, he is said to have composed some little works. Of these I have been able to find only one volume, brief indeed, but elegant:

    Letters to various persons, one book: “Surely you laugh because concerning me.”

    Of the rest I have seen nothing. He died while Anastasius was emperor, killed by Theodoric, king of Italy, at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord 524, in the second indiction.

    Avitus, bishop of Vienne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular letters, a theologian, rhetorician, and very famous poet, who in his time was valued no less for the purity of his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote not a few little works, both in verse and in prose, but very few have come to my knowledge. Of these the following are said to have been composed in elegant heroic meter:

    On the Origin of the World, one book. On Original Sin, one book. On the Judgment of God, one book. On the Flood of the World, one book. On the Crossing of the Red Sea, one book. Letters to various persons, nine books. Many Homilies, one book. And many others. He flourished under the emperors Zeno and Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

    Godelbertus, priest, learned in the divine Scriptures through constant exercise, rich in his reading of the ancients, and most learned in secular letters; a profound theologian, a famous orator, a notable poet, subtle in intellect, adorned in speech. He wrote in heroic meter a very famous work, running most elegantly through histories and allegories, from the beginning of the world up to the birth of the Virgin. The title of this work is:

    Allegories of the Scriptures, three books. But he wrote many other things. He flourished, as they say, in the times of the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

    Eugippius, priest and abbot, learned in the holy Scriptures, singularly devoted to reading the books of Saint Augustine, and sufficiently instructed in the letters of the secular arts; also renowned in life and conduct of monastic discipline. Some letters of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe are said to be addressed to him. He wrote certain necessary little works. Of these I have found only the following. He excerpted a large volume, containing three hundred chapters, from the books of blessed Augustine the bishop, addressed to Proba. Its prologue begins thus: one letter, “To the lady deservedly venerable.” The book itself thus: one book, “What I have written to you, honorable one.” His Rule of Monks, one book. He flourished under Emperor Anastasius, according to Honorius the priest; but according to Sigebert he flourished under Tiberius Constantine, in the times of Pope Pelagius II, in the year of the Lord 580.

    Benedict, the first abbot and founder of Monte Cassino, by homeland a man of Nursia, founder and chief of the monks of the West, a man of most holy conduct and illumined by the prophetic spirit. From his order afterward many most learned and most holy men became famous. He converted countless peoples from iniquity to Christ by word and example. From his order the Roman see has had eighteen pontiffs, more than two hundred cardinals, sixteen hundred archbishops in various churches, almost four thousand bishops, and outstanding abbots who became famous for doctrine, writings, or life, seventeen thousand. But those canonized or entered in the catalogue of saints, as in the monuments of the ancients

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 34

    we are instructed: fifteen thousand six hundred. Excepting those of whom, in all these matters, no accounts have come down to us. And concerning these illustrious men of our order we have already written four special books, in which we have recorded the names of some, though not of all. Saint Benedict, moreover, wrote, in lucid language and with outstanding discretion:

    The Rule of Monks, one book. It has seventy-four chapters.

    Under this rule twenty orders serve; these we have set out individually in the first book On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, although some are rare among us. He flourished under Justin the Elder, in the year of the Lord 530. And he died, as some maintain, in the year of the Lord 542, in the fifth indiction, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, when he was sixty-two years old, on the Saturday of holy Easter. But Marianus Scotus, an excellent computist, writes otherwise, saying as follows: If the holy father Benedict, abbot, as some write, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on the Saturday of holy Easter, he seems to have died in the year of the Lord 601. For unless [unclear] in the ninety-sixth year before that year, his death does not fit, because then, if born, he was very young. Therefore, according to this calculation of Marianus, the holy father Benedict died in the last year of the emperor Maurice, namely in the year of the Lord 601, at the age of more or less ninety, in the fourth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

    Boethius Manlius Severinus, ordinary consul, Roman, a philosopher, orator, and distinguished poet, learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, the most erudite of all men of his time, was the son-in-law of Symmachus the patrician. He was a man most richly imbued with Greek and Latin eloquence, since he translated many volumes both of Aristotle and of other philosophers from the Attic tongue into Latin; subtle in intellect, ready in understanding, and Catholic; in speech not inferior even to Tully. It is established that he had the friendship of Saint Benedict, and ate at his table on Monte Cassino with Tertullus, the senator and father of Placidus. He wrote many splendid volumes. Of these I have found the following:

    To Symmachus, his father-in-law, patrician of the city of Rome:

    On the Holy Trinity, one book. "Having investigated for a very long time."

    On the Unity of the Trinity, one book. "I ask whether the Father, the Son."

    On the Two Natures in Christ, one book. "Anxiously indeed and for a long time you."

    On the Faith, to John the deacon, one book. "The Christian faith of a new and."

    On Unity and the One, one book. "Unity is that by which each single thing."

    On the Isagoge of Porphyry, one book. "In the time of a winter year in [unclear]."

    On the Second Edition of the Same, one book. "This second [unclear] from."

    On the Categories of Aristotle, one book. "Having set out those things which pertain to the preliminary."

    On the Perihermenias of the Same, one book. "Great indeed [is] the book of this."

    On the Second Edition of the Same, six books. "Alexander in the commentaries."

    On Divisions, one book. "Which [unclear] great things for students."

    On Definitions, one book. "Of speaking and disputing."

    Introduction to Categorical Syllogisms, one book. "Many things the ancient philosophers."

    On Cicero’s Topics, six books. "At your exhortation, patrician."

    On Topical Differences, three books. "Every method of discussing which."

    On the Categorical Syllogism, one book. "Many things the ancient Greeks."

    On the Hypothetical Syllogism, one book. "Since in all matters of philosophy."

    On the Hebdomads, one book. "You ask that from the hebdomads."

    On Arithmetic, one book. "Among all things of ancient authority."

    On Music, five books. "Indeed every perception by sense."

    On the Consolation of Philosophy, five books. "Songs which with a certain zeal."

    On the Geometry of Euclid, three books. "But because, my patrician, geo-."

    On the Discipline of Scholars, one book. "Your intention knows concerning."

    On Rhetorical Places, one book.

    On the Predication of [unclear] of Passion, one book.

    Letters to Various Persons, one book.

    He says that he wrote also some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died in the same year as Symmachus the patrician and Pope John, under the emperor Anastasius, by order of King Theoderic at Ravenna, after a long exile, executed in prison, in the year of the Lord 524, in the second indiction. And under the name of Severinus he is said to have been entered in the catalogue of the saints.

    Hormisdas, pope, a Campanian by nation, presided over the Church after the pontiff Symmachus for nine years. He was a good, learned, and energetic man; having assembled a synod at Rome, he condemned the Eutychian heresy, and the Manichaeans, springing up again, he banished into exile after burning the books of their errors. Among other little works of his talent he wrote:

    A synodal decree, one book.

    To Justin Augustus, one letter: “Meanwhile, those things which pertain to the unity of the Church...”

    To the clergy of Second Syria, one letter: “When the letters of your affection had been read...”

    Several letters to various persons, one book.

    He died under Justin the Elder Augustus, in the year of the Lord 521, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of August. John succeeded him.

    Evodius, bishop of Ticinum, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of remarkable eloquence in both Greek and Latin, was sent by Pope Hormisdas to Constantinople in matters of the faith to Anastasius, the heretical emperor. After receiving many insults, he was expelled from the city together with his companions, Anastasius saying: “Why do you offer commands to us, who are under the dominion of no one? The Roman pontiff ought to obey us, not to give orders.” Evodius wrote to Pope Symmachus:

    On the Catholic Faith, one book.

    And certain other things.

    He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 510.

    Jordanes, from a monk bishop of the Goths, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and competently instructed in secular letters, gentle in disposition and plain in speech, an investigator of times and events and a notable writer, is said to have composed certain distinguished volumes. Of these, very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only:

    Histories, two books. In the first of these he reviewed the deeds of the Romans; in the second, the origin and deeds of the Goths down to the end of their kingdom.

    He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 530.

    Faustus, a monk and disciple of our most holy father Benedict, Italian by nation, a man venerable in knowledge and morals: when he was seven years old, he was offered by his parents to Father Benedict. At length, after the complete formation of his regular profession, he was sent with blessed Maurus into Gaul to build a monastery. There, after living for many years in great holiness, when Saint Maurus was dead he returned to Monte Cassino. At the request of the brethren, he wrote in quite clear eloquence to Boniface, the second pontiff of the Roman city:

    The Life of Saint Maurus the Abbot, one book.

    He flourished under the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

    Justinian the Great, emperor, sister’s son of Justin the Elder, reigned after him for thirty-eight years. He was a man of great and excellent talent, and rightly obtained a place among ecclesiastical writers, because he both published a very distinguished volume against the heretics, and, through the agency of John the patrician and the consuls Theophilus and Dorotheus, with admirable brevity corrected the Roman laws, which lay scattered in more than two thousand books. For, reducing all the constitutions of the emperors which were contained in many volumes to twelve books, he called it the Code.

    Again, reducing the laws of the individual magistrates and judges, which, as we have said, extended to almost two thousand books, to the number of fifty books in three volumes, he named it the Code of the Digest or Pandects. He also composed four books of Institutes, in which the kernel of the laws is contained and explained. The new laws also which he himself had established he reduced into one volume. Of all the books

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 35

    and so, of the works of the emperor Justinian that have come down to us, the following is the order set down, namely:

    The Code of Justinian: 12 books. “These things which necessarily [unclear].” The Digest, or Pandects: 50 books. The Institutes: 4 books. “Imperial majesty.” An Epitome of the Laws: 1 book. On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Eutyches: 3 books. Against the African Bishops: 1 book.

    Who would doubt that he also wrote other things, especially letters, both many and elegant, which have not come into our hands? He at last, in his old age, became mindless and foolish, and died in the year of the Lord 565, in the thirteenth indiction. Justin the Younger succeeded him.

    Dionysius, a Roman abbot, surnamed, as is reported, Exiguus: a man certainly great and most distinguished in talent and knowledge, learned in the sacred Scriptures, and nobly instructed in the discipline of secular letters; renowned in Greek and Latin eloquence; an outstanding computist and reckoner of times. He wrote some little works in the Latin language, of which I have found only the following: year 532.

    A Great Paschal Cycle: 1 book. “The reckoning of the paschal feast [unclear].” On the Reckoning of the Paschal Feast: 1 book.

    He also translated from Greek into Latin the Life of Saint Pachomius the abbot, and also the book of Gregory of Emesa On the Formation of Man, the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, and certain other things. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 532, which was the last year of the great paschal cycle, which, once completed, always returns to the same point. He therefore flourished under Justinian the Great, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Hecundus, bishop of Hermiane, richly learned in the sacred Scriptures by reading the ancients, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, is said to have written some volumes for the edification of readers. Of these, only a great and excellent work has come down to us, composed in an elegant style and furnished with great authorities from the ancients:

    In Defense of the Three Chapters: 12 books.

    He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Justinian, bishop of Valencia: a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of humane letters. From the same mother he had three brothers who were bishops, namely Justus, Nebridius, and Elpidius, learned and erudite men who composed various little works; these, however, have by no means come into our hands. He himself, among other things, composed for a certain man named Rusticus:

    On Five Questions: 1 book. And certain other things.

    He flourished in Spain under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Prigius, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain: learned in the divine Scriptures, most erudite in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech. He expounded the sacred Scriptures so gloriously and profoundly that, in comparison with him, the ancient writers would seem not to have expounded them. Of his little works there survives a notable volume, subtle in meaning and splendid in speech:

    On the Apocalypse of John: 1 book. On the Song of Songs: 1 book.

    He also published many other things, which have not come into our hands.

    Book

    He flourished in the times of Theodotus, king of the Goths, under Justinian the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 530.

    Cassiodorus, monk and abbot of the monastery near Ravenna, a man very learned in divine Scripture and in secular letters, easily the most erudite of all in his time, shone forth no less renowned for holiness than for knowledge. He was first chancellor of Theoderic, king of Italy, and a senator of Ravenna, and consul of the city of Rome; afterward, despising the vain honors of the world, for love of God he became a monk. Then, directing the study of humane letters to the exposition of holy Scripture, he composed many most elegant treatises. Of his works the following are reported. In the person both of himself and of King Theoderic he wrote:

    Letters to various persons, 28 books.

    On the Nature of the Soul, 1 book. “When now of the work undertaken...”

    On the whole Psalter, 1 book. “Blessed is the man,” etc. Very beautiful.

    Instruction in Divine Readings, 2 books. “Since the pursuits of secular letters...”

    On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Solomon, inspired by the divine...”

    Instruction in Secular Letters, 9 books. “Our intention is concerning the art...”

    He compiled the Tripartite History, 12 books. Very useful at the beginning of the book.

    Catalogue of the Roman Consuls, 1 book.

    On Etymologies, 1 book.

    The Fore-Noted Priest, 1 book.

    On Figures and Tropes, 1 book.

    Memorial of the Scriptures, 1 book.

    On Orthography, 1 book.

    Expositions on the Apocalypse, 1 book.

    On the Canonical Epistles, 7 books.

    On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book.

    He also composed many other things which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of Justin the elder down almost to the end of the reign of Justin the younger, being more than 95 years of age, in the year of the Lord 575.

    Arator, subdeacon of the most holy Roman Church, a man practiced in divine Scriptures and nobly learned in the literature of the secular disciplines, powerful in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, clear and polished in speech, wrote a very distinguished volume, composed in meter, to a certain abbot Florian:

    On the Acts of the Apostles, 3 books. “That Judaea, polluted by the crime of its own...”

    To Abbot Florian, 1 letter. “You who by merits...”

    To Pope Vigilius, 1 letter. “With watery walls of wars...”

    And certain other things which I have not seen.

    This Arator, a very distinguished poet and notable theologian, offered the book on the Acts of the Apostles which he had composed in elegant meter to Pope Vigilius before the confession of Saint Peter, on the seventh Ides of April, in the presence of many bishops and learned men; and, at the pontiff’s command, he recited a large part of it publicly before all. As the hour was passing, Pope Vigilius handed the book to the venerable Surgentius, the primicerius, to be placed in the archive, so that he might complete its reading at a free time. All the learned men earnestly begged his holiness to order the book to be read before them in its entirety. When he had ordered this to be done in the church of Saint Peter ad Vincula, a great crowd of religious, nobles, and laymen assembled; and as Arator himself recited in distinct words, both books were heard four times, since on one day only half of a book was read because of the continual repetitions which the listeners demanded with manifold favor. Where in the present times is there such study of letters? Where is the love of saving knowledge? Our religious men, and nobles, and also clerical pontiffs listen not to books but to revenues; they cultivate not letters but avarice. Now Antimachus reads many poems, and as individuals withdraw, scarcely a single Plato is found to remain. But we are now speaking out of season about these matters.

    Arator flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers

    Fol. 36

    Victor, bishop of the [Tunnunensian?] church in Africa, a man learned in divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, was banished into exile in Egypt by the emperor Justinian and by Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, because of his defense of the Three Chapters. From there, summoned again to Constantinople, when he resisted the emperor and the bishop, the detractors of those same Chapters, he was sent to be guarded in a monastery of the same city; and, as they say, he remained in that same condemnation and died. Among other works of his talent he wrote, from the beginning of the world down to the first year of the reign of Justin the younger, a very useful History concerning deeds and ecclesiastical wars:

    History, 1 book.

    For the Defense of the Three Chapters, 1 book.

    And certain other things.

    He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Gregory, the first pope, from being a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, Roman by homeland: after the pontificate of Pelagius he sat in the chair of Peter for thirteen years and six months. He was most learned in the divine Scriptures, and indeed very learned in secular letters; prince of theologians, splendor of philosophers, and light of rhetoricians; upright and most holy in life and conduct. While he was explaining the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit several times appeared to him in visible form, and by invisible teaching disclosed to him the hidden mysteries of those same Scriptures. At Rome, at Saint Peter’s, he held a synod of twenty-four bishops, established many things for the utility of the Church, and promulgated a decree on the immunity of monasteries. He wrote several necessary volumes. Of these the following are reported: To Leander, bishop of Seville.

    Moralia on the Book of Job, thirty-five books: “Among many it is often asked.” On Pastoral Care, two books: “The weight of pastoral care.” Dialogues on the Miracles of the Saints, four books: “On a certain day, too much [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, four books: “After [unclear] from the joys of paradise.” On Ezekiel the Prophet, two books: “By the inspiration of almighty God.” Homilies on the Gospels, forty, in two books: “Our Lord and Redeemer.” A Brief Explanation of the Four Gospels, four books: “Matthew, as in the order.” On the Seven Penitential Psalms, two books. Letters to Various Persons, ten books: “Gregory, bishop, servant.” Rationale of Divine Things. [unclear]. On the Sacraments.

    While he was still a deacon, on behalf of Pope Pelagius he wrote a very distinguished letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; this letter is not found among his letters. He is also said to have written very many other works: namely, on the Prophets, on the Books of Kings, also on the books of Moses, and on other sacred Scriptures. After his death, before they had yet been copied, his most wicked rivals, envying his glory and holiness, burned them with fire, as John the Deacon laments in the book of his life. The most blessed Pope Gregory died in the second year of the emperor Phocas, which was the year of the Lord six hundred and nine, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth Ides of March, shining with many miracles.

    Leander, bishop of Seville, from being a monk, Carthaginian by homeland, from the province of Spain, born of his father Severianus: a most studious man, nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, sweet in speech, most excellent in talent, and also holy in life and conduct and beloved of God. By his preaching and effort Hermingild, son of Leuvigild, the Arian king of the Goths, was brought back to the confession of the orthodox faith, and on the vigil of Easter, slain by his heretical father, received the crown of martyrs. His brother Richard, as soon as after his father’s death he had taken up the kingdom, at Leander’s urging and preaching, renounced heresy and converted the whole people of the Visigoths subject to him to the Catholic faith. To this blessed Leander, blessed Gregory dedicated the volumes of his commentaries on Job. Leander himself also wrote some little works, of which there are reported

    BOOK

    the following. When, on account of the Catholic faith, he had been banished into exile by the Arians, he wrote:

    Against heretics, two books. Against the ordinances of the Arians, one book. On virginity, to Florentina, one book. Prayers in a twofold edition on the psalm[s], one book. On contempt for death, to his brother, one book. On the praise of sacrifices, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

    But he also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 590, under the emperor Maurice. He died under Reccared, the most devout prince of the Goths, renowned for miracles.

    Priscian the grammarian, by homeland a Caesarean, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, held in great esteem with Chosroes, king of the Persians, wrote certain distinguished volumes on the grammatical art, which among the ancients were held in great authority. Of these the following are reported:

    To Julian the patrician. On the parts of speech, two books. On construction, one book. On accents, one book. On cosmography, one book. On natural questions, to [unclear], one book.

    He is also said to have written some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished, as some think, in the times of Chosroes, king of the Persians, and of the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 620.

    Marcus, a monk and disciple of our holy father Benedict, and most dearly loved by him, a man learned in the divine scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, an orator and distinguished poet, renowned in morals and manner of life, wrote, after the blessed Pope Gregory, adding some things, running most elegantly in heroic verse:

    The Life of Saint Benedict, one book. And certain other things.

    He flourished down to the reign of Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.

    Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine scriptures and most learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent and polished in speech, excelling all the doctors of his age in verse and prose, having been freed from pain in the eyes by [Saint Martin?], came to Tours to his tomb to give thanks; and, having gone on to Poitiers, he was first ordained priest and then bishop there, and was renowned for great learning and religion. He wrote many useful and devout little works in elegant verse. Of these I have seen only the following. To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians and captive of the king of the Franks, afterwards abbess of the monastery of Poitiers, in hexameter verse:

    The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians, one book. “[The condition?] of war, a sorrowful lot.” To [Jovinus?] on Radegund, one book. “You who eagerly lick the Aonian [unclear].” To Justin the Younger, one book. “Glory of the highest [Father?] and of the Son, and [unclear].” To Sophia Augusta, one book. “To whom, marrying one equal in merits [unclear].” On Radegund’s psalm, one book. “After the ashes of the fatherland and [unclear].” In praise of Bishop Martin, one book. “When he was spreading apostolic light.” On the venerable Bishop Leontius, one book. “Among whom [unclear] begot [a ray?].” On praise of the same, one book. “Let every age know [unclear].” Seventy-seven hymns, one book. “Let every age know [that] [unclear] has come.”

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 37

    On the miracles of Saint Martin: four books. The life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers: one book. To Oporicus on his own life: one book. The life of a holy bishop: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Poems to friends: one book. “The king, the summit of the region,” etc. He also composed many other works, which, since they are short, I have not wished to mark under the name of books. For he wrote many epitaphs and brief verses, which I have seen. He flourished under Justin the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 570.

    Gregory, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk and once a disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of the Auvergnats, a learned and noble man, and also gentle and humble, was of such great holiness and purity that even in life he shone with miracles. When he visited the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was received by the blessed Pope Gregory with the greatest reverence and charity, as a truly holy man and a special friend, uniquely beloved by him. He wrote several volumes in a simple and plain style, of which there survive:

    On the praise of the holy martyrs: one book. On the life of certain confessors: two books. On the miracles of Saint Julian the martyr: one book. On the miracles of Saint Martin: four books. History of the Franks: ten books. An epitome of the same: one book. Chronicle of ecclesiastical history: one book. The other works which he composed have not yet come to our knowledge through reading. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

    Martin, bishop, formerly ruler and abbot of the monastery of Dumio, a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, coming from the regions of the East into Gaul, converted the people of the Sueves by teaching and miracles from Arian impiety to the right faith; he established rules of orthodox faith, founded monasteries, and reformed churches. He wrote to Mito, king of Galicia, on the four virtues which are called cardinal, an instructive volume which he wished to entitle:

    The Form of an Honorable Life: one book. A book of letters full of the cultivation of virtues: one book. And certain other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Theodemir, king of the Sueves, while Justinian Augustus governed the Constantinopolitan empire, in the year of the Lord 540.

    Paterius, notary and secundicerius of the Roman Church, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gathered all the testimonies of divine Scripture by which the blessed Pope Gregory clarified the obscure points of his exposition, and published three books: two, namely, on testimonies of the Old Testament, and one on the Testament; and he entitled the codex itself:

    Testimony: four books. “When of the most blessed and apostolic...” I have seen nothing concerning the rest. He flourished at Rome at the same time when Pope Gregory presided over the universal Church, and at his urging he compiled the aforesaid volume, while Maurice Augustus held the empire and after him Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

    Columbanus, first founder and abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, a Scot by nation, a man of outstanding holiness, merit, and learning, father of many thousands of monks and founder of several monasteries, an excellent sower of the divine word, coming from Ireland into Gaul and Germany, increased divine worship, monasteries, and servants, as once the chief of the Druids had done. While he was still rather young he devoted great study to sacred letters, so that he wrote in an elegant style:

    Book

    Commentaries on the whole Psalter, one book. And certain letters to the brothers. He died under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 598, in the first indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

    John, bishop of Constantinople, a Cappadocian by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, of inestimable holiness, so intent upon alms and works of piety that the emperor Maurice, moved against him by a zeal of avarice, ordered all the poor and beggars to be expelled from the city of Constantinople. He wrote in Greek to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, and certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

    Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, after many exercises of study, was killed at Constantinople by his rivals with a cup of poison under the emperor Maurice. Sudden death did not harm him, since Scripture says: “The just man, by whatever death he may have been overtaken, shall be in a place of refreshment.” For then he truly begins to live, when, adorned with good works, he goes through death to Christ, never to die. He wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, of which I have not yet deserved to see any. The following are said to be his: On the sacrament of baptism, one book; Letters to various persons, one book; and certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 590.

    Severus, bishop of the city of Malaga, formerly the companion and colleague of the aforesaid bishop Licinianus, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in intellect and distinguished in speech, wrote against Vincentius, bishop of the city of Zaragoza, who had passed from the Catholic faith into Arian depravity: A Correction, one book; On virginity, to his sister, one book; Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished in the year of the Lord 580, under the emperor Maurice, under whom he died.

    Eutropius, bishop of the church of Valencia, formerly abbot of the monastery of Servitanum of the order of Saint Benedict, to whom Licinianus, while still living in the aforesaid monastery, wrote many letters, a man magnificently learned both in divine writings and in secular letters, and excellently imbued with monastic disciplines. While he was still abbot he wrote to Bishop Licinianus why, after infants have been baptized, the triple anointing with chrism follows afterwards, one book; On the correction of monks, one book; and several letters to various persons. He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

    John, bishop of Gerona, formerly a monk of our order, a Goth by nation, from the province of Lusitania, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, also distinguished in morals and conduct, learned and famous in Greek and Latin speech: when, as a young man, he went to Constantinople out of love of learning, after seven years had passed he returned to Spain. When King Leovigild could not bring him over to Arian impiety, he condemned him to a fairly harsh exile for ten years. Recalled from there by the most Christian king [Reccaredus?], he founded a monastery, where by word and example he showed his brothers the path of regular discipline. He wrote: An Exhortation to monks, one book; Additions to the chronicle, one book; [unclear], of which we spoke above: a little work [unclear], one book.

    ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS. Fol. 38.

    He composed also many other [works], which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under [Richard / Reccared?], most Christian king of the Visigoths, in Spain, in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

    Maximus, bishop of the city of Saragossa, learned in the divine Scriptures and not moderately erudite in secular [letters], prompt in talent and polished in eloquence, excelling in verse [and] prose, published in either style quite illustrious volumes, which have as yet by no means come to the notice of our reading. But there is reported [as] his a notable volume, a pleasant work: On the deeds of the Goths in Spain: 1 book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

    Jonas, a monk, disciple of Saint Columbanus the abbot, companion of his pilgrimage, a Scot by nation, a studious man, erudite, renowned for knowledge, no less venerable for religion than for learning, wrote in composed speech, at the request of the brothers, for the edification of many: The Life of Saint Columbanus: 1 book. The Life of Saint Attala the monk: 1 book. The Life of Saint Eustasius the abbot: 1 book. He flourished under the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630.

    Leontius, bishop of the city of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, also most renowned in life and conversation, a prelate worthy of God. He wrote, among the other little works of his talent, a notable volume on the acts [and] admirable conversation of that patriarch of Alexandria who, on account of [his] incredible piety [and] compassion toward the poor, was surnamed John the Almsgiver: 1 book. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

    Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, second to none of his time in secular letters, subtle in talent, clear in sense, composed in eloquence, excelling in verse [and] prose, shone forth no less distinguished for sanctity than for learning. He is called "the Younger" to distinguish him from the elder, bishop of Cordoba, of whom we made mention above, or also from another, bishop of Seville, who preceded him. This Isidore the Younger wrote many illustrious little works, of which I have found only the following. To Braulio the bishop: Of Etymologies: 20 books. ["Discipline [is so called] from learning…"] On Genesis, allegorically: 1 book. ["The history of the sacred law…"] On Exodus: 1 book. ["Certain mysteries…"] On Numbers: 1 book. ["Therefore this one book…"] On Leviticus: 1 book. ["The following Leviticus book…"] On Deuteronomy: 1 book. ["The book of Deuteronomy [is] found…"] On Joshua: 1 book. ["After the death of Moses, the servant…"] On Judges: 1 book. ["The history of the Judges…"] On Kings: 3 books. ["After the book of Judges there follows…"] On Ruth: 1 book. On Paralipomenon [Chronicles]: 1 book. On Ezra [and] Nehemiah: 3 books. On Tobias: 1 book. On Judith: 1 book. On Esther: 1 book. On Job: 1 book. On the Psalter: 1 book. On the Proverbs of Solomon: 1 book. On Ecclesiastes: 1 book. On the Song of Songs: 1 book. On the book of Wisdom: 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus: 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet: 1 book. On Jeremiah: 1 book. On Ezekiel: 1 book. On Daniel the prophet: 1 book. On the twelve minor prophets: 12 books. On the Maccabees: 2 books. On the four Gospels: 4 books. The book of generation, etc.: 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul: 13 books. On the canonical epistles: 7 books.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 39

    Sermons to monks, one book, “I fear in Christ, venera...” Decree of the three councils of Arles, three books, “Concerning the rest I have found nothing.”

    In the third sermon, which is on the monk’s battle against vices, he acknowledges both himself and those to whom he speaks as professed monks of the order of the Rule of our most holy father Benedict. He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantine, son of Heraclius, and of his sons, in the year of the Lord 670; under them he presided gloriously over the synod of Arles.

    Audoenus, who was also called Dado, bishop of Rouen, a Gaul by nation, brother of Saint Ado the monk, a learned and most holy man, founder of the monastery of Rebais, since he was learned both in the holy Scriptures and also in secular letters, wrote in a very elegant style to Rupertus, bishop of Paris:

    The Life of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, three books, and certain other things.

    He flourished with great holiness, virtues, and signs in the times of the above-mentioned emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 660.

    Theodorus, seventh archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated by Pope Vitalian, a Greek by nation, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a monk of our order in the city of Rome, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech, excellent also in verse and prose, renowned no less for holiness than for knowledge: after holding a synod in England, he made many provisions for the English church. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote an outstanding work on the kind of penance to be imposed on those who had offended in many crimes. The title of this work is:

    The Penitential of Theodore, one book; some letters to various persons.

    He died, not without a reputation for holiness, under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 690, in the third indiction, in the seventy-eighth year of his age, and the twenty-second of his episcopate.

    Leo, the second pope, a Sicilian by nation, sat in the chair of Peter after Agatho for only eleven months.
