    Campanus, a Lombard by nation, a philosopher and astronomer, in everyone’s opinion most celebrated in his time, acute in talent, scholastic in speech, and also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished calculator and computist, produced not a few little works of his talent, the reading of which will not be contemptible to the rulers of churches. Of these I have read only the following, a great and distinguished work:

    On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. “One of these asked me.”

    On the Composition of the Quadrant, one book. “You should know that the circle [unclear].”

    Also a Calendar, one book.

    He also composed many other works in astronomy, which have not come into our hands.

    He is said to have flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1030.

    Helpericus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, and distinguished astronomer, subtle in talent and composed in speech, wrote some little works both in meter and in prose. Of these I have been able to find only the excellent work:

    On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. “When, as an adolescent, with our brothers.”

    Also On Music, one book.

    Of the rest I have seen nothing.

    He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year 1069.

    [Berthorius?], abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the sacred Scriptures and nobly instructed in the discipline of secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and physician. Before his conversion he is said to have written many little works in his faculty. But afterward, changing his study and being made a physician of the soul as well, he wrote for the edification of his brothers:

    Elegant Sermons, one book.

    He also produced other additional and various treatises, knowledge of which has not come to me.

    Rogerius, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, to whom Guimundus of Aversa, bishop, while still established in the monastery, is said to have written three books against Berengar, a learned man and instructed in both divine and secular letters, described for the edification of many, in sufficiently lucid speech:

    The Life of Bruno, Bishop of Cologne, one book.

    And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1040.

    BOOK.

    Algerus, from [being] a scholastic [a] monk of Corbie [Corvey] in Saxony, a Teuton by nation, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man exercised by continual study in the holy Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, and moreover magnificently learned in secular letters, cautious in talent and eloquent enough, strong in verse and prose. He wrote, in a quite urbane style, a distinguished volume: On the sacrament of the altar: book. On grace and free will: book. And certain letters. He is said to have written also several others, which have not come into our hands. ["Because the saints, from the body and…"; "It is to be known that free will…"] He flourished in the times of Conrad the Younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1030.

    Albert, monk of Metz, of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man skilled by continual exercise in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of the arts of humanity which we call liberal. That he might transmit his name to posterity, he wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, of which there is reported a brief but useful work containing the history of the deeds of his time, which he dedicated To the bishop of Metz: 1 book. And certain others. He flourished in the times of Conrad the Younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1030.

    Eckebert, clerk of the church of Liège, a Teuton by nation, elegantly learned in the divine Scriptures, and instructed to perfection in the disciplines of secular letters, wrote both in meter and in prose some little works, by which he transmitted his name to the notice of posterity. Of these there is extant a volume composed in elegant meter, which he entitled On rustic riddles: 1 book. On the same matter, another, larger: book. And certain others. He flourished in the times of Henry III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1060.

    Leo, pope, the ninth, from [being] bishop of the city of the Leuci which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, sat in the chair of Peter, after Damasus, for six years; previously called Bruno, a learned and holy man. He wrote some illustrious little works, in which the gracefulness of eloquence and the sublimity of the sentences are deservedly commended. Of these are these: To Constantine the monk-emperor: On extirpating heresies: 1 book. To the patriarch of Constantinople: book. Against the errors of the Greeks: book. To the bishops of Africa and Egypt: book. Of letters, to various [persons]: book. He dies under Henry, king the third, emperor the second, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the 7th indiction, shining with many miracles.

    [Humbert,] most erudite in the [holy] Scriptures, and nobly learned in secular letters, renowned in talent and eloquence, whom Pope Leo IX, on account of [his] knowledge of letters, led with him to Rome and ordained a cardinal bishop; [and who,] sent by him to Constantinople to confute the heresies of the Greeks, so confuted and overcame Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk, in the presence of the emperor Constantine and the patriarch Michael, that he anathematized his book which he had written against the Latin church, and cast it with his own hand into the fire to be burned. And whatever he there said or did in disputing, he luminously set down, under the name of "a Roman and a Constantinopolitan," in the manner Of dialogues: book. He wrote also certain others. He flourished under Henry the emperor, the second, in the year of the Lord 1050.

    Anselm, monk of Rheims, of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man having a talent exercised in the divine Scriptures. He wrote certain little works of his study, which have as yet by no means come into our hands. And among others

    On Ecclesiastical Writers

    he compiled into one volume the deeds of Pope Leo IX performed throughout Gaul in councils and assemblies, so that he might make known with how great authority he held a synod at Reims or in other cities; with what industry and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what severity he corrected sinners; and how divine power cooperated with him. This was sufficiently evident in one case at the synod of Reims, where, when the bishop of Freising acted contumaciously against apostolic authority, by God’s vengeance he suddenly became mute before the eyes of all. He wished to entitle this work:

    The Itinerary of Pope Leo: one book.

    He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

    Lanfranc, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Caen, of the order of Saint Benedict, an Italian by nation from the city of Pavia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, especially in dialectic, in the opinion of all the most learned man of his time, renowned no less for holiness than for knowledge, left excellent monuments of his talent. Of these I have found only the following:

    On all the epistles of Paul the Apostle: fourteen books, [unclear]. Against Berengar: one book. “Lanfranc, by the mercy of God, [unclear].” The Deeds of Count William: one book.

    Of the rest I have found nothing.

    He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

    Peter Damian, formerly a monk of the divine father Benedict, bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, gentle and acute in intellect, calm and composed in speech, quite fit for persuasion; he shone forth as distinguished and renowned no less for holiness than for learning. Following the example of the great bishop Gregory, out of love for solitude and quiet he left his episcopate, after he had governed it vigorously for some years, and returned to his monastery; thereafter he spent his life with his brothers in tranquility of mind. But when he was reproved by the supreme pontiff with a charitable rebuke as to why, being a useful and suitable man, he had abandoned the episcopate out of love for private salvation, he published apologetic writings addressed to the three Roman pontiffs succeeding one another: Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII. In these, humbly excusing his deed by authority, reason, and example, he calmed their minds.

    Of his minor works the following are reported. To Leo the hermit, on whether a solitary person praying the canonical hours ought also to say “The Lord be with you,” when there is no one to answer: an instructive little work entitled:

    The Lord Be with You: one book. “To lord Leo, from love of heavenly...” Apologetic: three books. “To his lord Nicholas, universal...” On the Incontinence of Priests: one book. “Lately, [unclear] with certain bishops...” Rule of Solitaries: one book. “I address you, O hares...” Exhortation to Monks: one book. “While by the fervor of holy [conversion?]...” Miracles of His Own Time: one book. “To the brothers in the [Gangangensian?] hermitage...” On the Progress of Monks: one book. “To the most beloved Gerard, [unclear]...” Antilogion against the Jews: one book. “Hugh, abbot of Cluny, this...” On the Avarice of Prelates: one book. “To Blanca, once a countess, now...” Life of Abbot Odilo: one book. “For it must indeed be weighed, since now...” On the Terror of Death: one book. Against Simoniac Bishops: one book. Against a Certain Bishop: one book. Gratissimus or Probatissimus: one book. “To lord H. of the see of Ravenna, [unclear]”

    BOOK

    Of Rhetorical Declamation: one book. On the Natures of Certain Animals: one book. On Flora and Lucilla: one book. On Cassian the martyr: one book. On Saint Boniface: one book. On Saint Anastasius: one book. Of sermons and homilies: one book. And many other things which I have not seen. He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1050.

    Bruno, archbishop of the Ruthenians, formerly a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, outstanding by birth, holy and in every way worthy of God, since, preaching the catholic faith in Prussia, he lawfully received the crown of martyrdom from the enemies of Christ. He wrote some excellent little works of his own talent, of which there survive commentaries:

    On Genesis: two books.

    And certain other things. He suffered at the hands of the Prussians under Saint Henry, who was the second king of this name and the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1008, in the sixth indiction. After afflicting him with many tortures, cutting off his feet and hands, they finally, by beheading him, made him a martyr of Christ.

    Erhard, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned by continual exercise, subtle in intellect and ready in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering homilies to the people. By expounding the divine Scriptures he made his name known; by frequent exposition of the same he became an outstanding teacher. He wrote, moreover, little works of reading not to be despised, among which they report:

    Commentaries on Genesis: one book. On Exodus: one book. On Leviticus: one book. On Numbers: one book. On Deuteronomy: one book. Also of homilies: one book.

    He also published some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

    Bernold, priest of the church of Constance in Swabia, German by nation, a devout man, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, clear in intellect and polished in speech, left some little works of his study, which nevertheless have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He is said to have composed, for the benefit of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, a volume which he entitled:

    The Roman Order: one book.

    He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

    Marbod, bishop of Rennes, very zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned by reading of the ancients, and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote in both styles not a few volumes, which can no less please readers than profit them. Among these there stands out a notable work which he composed in elegant meter with a threefold sense:

    On the Song of Songs: one book. The Passion of the Theban Martyrs, in verse: one book.

    And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

    Marianus, a monk of Fulda, of the Order of Saint Benedict, Scottish by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, a historian and distinguished computist, leaving his own country, came into Germany as a pilgrim for love of Christ. First at Cologne, at Saint Martin’s, he was made a monk and, from desire for solitude, enclosed himself; he stayed there for two years. Afterwards, transferred to Fulda, he remained enclosed there for twelve years, until at last on account of the learning of the holy

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 52

    [unclear] by order of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda; moving to Mainz, for seventeen years at Saint Martin’s, again remaining enclosed, he was held in great honor by all. He wrote, from the beginning of the world down to his own times:

    An outstanding Chronicle, three books, “We are instructed by the divine …”

    On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book, “There was in the days of Herod …”

    On Computation also, one book, and certain other works. He died under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the fifty-eighth year of his age; and he was buried at Mainz at Saint Martin’s, in the greater church, not without a reputation for holiness.

    Henricus, bishop of Vercelli, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, made his name known to posterity by writing, although his little works have not come to the knowledge of our reading. In that discord which existed between Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, and Henry, Emperor III or King IV, he wrote, in the person of Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, while he was still a cleric at Trier, to the same Pope Gregory a volume furnished with divine Scriptures: not rebuking him, but entreating him as an elder, as a father, with the friendly affection of one grieving, setting before him all the things which talkative rumor had spread abroad that he had done or said against the right of laws, divine law, and equity. He entitled it:

    On the Discord between the Kingdom and the Priesthood, one book.

    Concerning the rest I have found nothing. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year 1080.

    Theodericus, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written certain little works of reading not to be despised. Of these, few have come to my knowledge. They are read to Richard, abbot of Fulda:

    On the Life of Saint Benedict, one book, “When of heavenly sacraments …”

    On the Translation of the Body of the Same, one book, “When for a long time the Lombard people …”

    Letters also to various persons, one book.

    He also composed many other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come down to us. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

    Adam, abbot of Perseigne, of the order of the holy father Benedict, learned in the divine Scriptures by constant exercise, rich in the reading of the ancients, and sufficiently instructed in the knowledge of secular letters, of very celebrated reputation in delivering declamations and homilies, transmitted his name with praise to posterity by composing various treatises. There are extant his devout and useful:

    Sermons to the Brothers, one book.

    On Saints, on Various Subjects, one book.

    He is also said to have expounded certain treatises of Sacred Scripture, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent; but they have not come to my knowledge.

    Anselm, bishop of Lucca, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not meanly instructed in secular letters, the tireless co-worker of Pope Gregory VII, an outstanding defender against Guibert, who had been subordinated to him by Henry, so that by the authority of the law of the Scriptures he defended all his deeds, sayings, or writings against Henry the emperor. He left very famous monuments of a great talent, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

    On Jeremiah the Prophet, one book.

    On the Psalter also, one book.

    Against Guibert the Antipope, one book.

    And several letters to various persons, one book.

    He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

    Book [unclear]

    Willelmus, abbot of Merseburg, of the order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, practiced in verse and prose; after he had spent some time applying himself to letters at the University of Paris, he returned to his homeland and was made scholasticus of the church of Bamberg. Then, considering that the glory of the world passes away with time, having despised the world, he put on the monk in the monastery of Fulda for love of Christ; and at last, as he increased in merits, he was consecrated abbot in the monastery of Saint Peter at Merseburg, and made his name known to posterity by writing. Of his little works I have read only a volume composed in a beautiful variety, in mixed meter and verse with prose, on the nuptials of Christ and the Church:

    On the Song of Songs, two books, “I behold the studies of the elders …”

    Concerning the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1070.

    Franco, scholasticus of the church of Liège, a German by nation, a man splendidly learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly trained in secular discipline, an outstanding philosopher, astronomer, and computist, and no less venerable for religion than for knowledge. He is said to have composed several treatises on the sacred Scriptures, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He wrote to Hermann II, archbishop of Cologne, a subtle and excellent work:

    On the squaring of the circle, one book. On ecclesiastical computus, one book. And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

    Bernard, a monk of Cluny of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man practiced in the sacred Scriptures by constant meditation, and not ignorant of secular literature, conspicuous also for religion and uprightness of morals, at the command of the venerable Abbot Hugh gathered all the customs of the monastery of Cluny into one volume in lucid language, prefixing this title to the work:

    The Customs of Cluny, one book. He also wrote other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

    Bernard, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote to Hartwin, archbishop of Magdeburg, in a lucid style indeed, but against Henry IV:

    Against Henry IV, one book. [unclear]: a volume. And other things which I have not seen. He flourished in the times of the same Emperor Henry, in the year 1070.

    Ivo, bishop of Chartres, formerly provost of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, of the Order of Regular Canons of the divine father Augustine, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and a most cautious interpreter of the canons of the holy fathers and of general councils, and no less revered for holiness than for knowledge; he magnificently reformed his order, long in collapse. After Burchard, bishop of Worms, he wrote from the canons of the saints a concise decretum, which jurists used before the times of Gratian, which he entitled:

    Panormia, ten books. Ecclesiastical Excerpts. Letters to various persons, one book. Ivo, to the [unclear] church of Chartres. And certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

    Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular teachings, acute in intellect and very eloquent in speech, once a disciple of Berengar of Tours, but an assailant of error, who endured many persecutions and tribulations, even imprisonment, for ecclesiastical liberty. He wrote in both styles, namely metrical and prose, certain distinguished little works, of which few have so far been able to come to our knowledge by reading. He wrote in elegant metre a very beautiful and useful exposition:

    On the whole office of the Mass, one book. “I wished to write, since my...” On his exile, one book. “Recently I was wealthy in...”

    On Ecclesiastical Writers Folio 53

    On the misery of this life: one book. On the sacrament of the altar: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. A hymn and prayers in various meters: one book. He included an epitaph of Berengar, once his teacher, in fifty-two verses. He also wrote many other things still unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

    Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, of the Order of Saint Benedict, once a hearer and disciple of Lanfranc, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular [unclear] and skill second to none in his time; upright and most holy in life and conduct; devout in mind; eloquent in speech; vigorous in action; angelic in countenance; mature in bearing; exemplary in his course of life; constant in the study of the Scriptures; and adorned and distinguished by every virtue. He wrote almost countless little works, among which the following are reported:

    Against the gentiles, why concerning man: one book. On the incarnation of the Word, against the Jews: one book. On the virginal conception: one book. Proslogion: one book. Monologion: one book. On the Holy Spirit, against the Greeks: one book. On the fall of the devil: one book. On the diversity of the sacraments: one book. On leavened and unleavened bread: one book. On the will of God: one book. On the Holy Trinity: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On peace and concord: one book. On free choice: one book. On grace and free choice: one book. A dialogue on truth: one book. On likenesses: one book. On the measurement of the cross: one book. Meditations: one book. Meditations on the passion of God: one book. On the blessed life: one book. On blessed sufficiency: one book. On good occupation: one book. On the praises of Saint Mary: one book. The spur of love: one book. On behalf of the fool: one book. Against the fool: one book. On the misery of man: one book. On Antichrist: one book. Dialogue of a Christian and a gentile: one book. On the ways of the beatitudes: one book. On the members attributed to God: one book. On the sacraments and divine offices: one book. Proverbs, that is, On the house of [unclear]: one book. On the Hexaemeron: one book. To Archbishop Lanfranc: one book. On the grammarian: one book.

    “We are taken from the midst by the fates.” “Often also [unclear] by many.” “To the lord and [unclear] the church.” “To whom in all things of your religious [unclear].” “Come now, little man, flee.” “[Unclear], I am one nature.” “[Unclear] by the Greeks and [unclear].” “That saying of the Apostle: What do you have which...” “To the lord and friend Walram.” “Anselm, servant of the church of Canterbury.” “Human reason, which concerning God...” “To whom free choice may seem...” “On those three questions.” “That God is truth.” “The will is understood in three ways.” “That by ordering your son Christ...” “Lord my God, grant to the heart...” “Christian soul, soul from grave...” “Jesus of Nazareth [unclear] to the Jews.” “They doubt whether it is or...” “That [unclear] reproaches me.” “My life terrifies me and...” “Wherever sacred Scripture...” “The celebration of Mass in common.” “This house in which I dwell.”

    On Saint John the Baptist: one book. On the Assumption of Saint Mary: a homily. To William of Hirsau: a letter. A book of letters to various persons. On Original Sin: one book. Also some sermons. But he is also said to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1080.

    William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of Saint Be[unclear], wrote some letters: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, in secular letters inferior to no one among the Germans in his time; a philosopher, astronomer, distinguished musician, most holy in life and conduct, who is read to have shone with many miracles. He reformed regular discipline, which had long since collapsed in many monasteries of Germany. Therefore, for the preservation of monastic observance, he wrote from the ancient statutes: Constitutions of Monks: one book. On the Tones of Music: one book. On the Clock: one book. On the Correction of the Psalter: one book. To Saint Anselm of Canterbury: a letter. A book of letters to various persons. He also published some other things, which through the negligence of the ancients have fallen into oblivion. He died under the emperor Henry III, but as king of the Romans the fourth, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of July. He was buried in the middle of the church of the apostles, with a great reputation for holiness.

    Gilbert, provost of the monastery of West[unclear] in England, of the Order of Saint Benedict, hearer and disciple of Anselm of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect, cautious in speech, made his name known to posterity by writing, when he composed certain necessary little works. Of these the following are reported: A Disputation against the Jews, To the blessed Anselm, bishop: one book. On the Prophet Isaiah: one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV with Anselm, in the year of the Lord 1090.

    Ontherus, a monk of Elwangen, of the Order of Saint Benedict, skilled in the divine Scriptures by constant exercise, nobly taught in the disciplines of secular letters, a famous theologian and poet, subtle in intellect, polished in speech, wrote in meter and prose certain excellent volumes. Of these few have come to my knowledge. There is extant a volume of his in elegant meter: On the Passion of Saint Cyriacus: one book. And certain letters. He flourished in the times of King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

    Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo in the diocese of Liege, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. In both styles he wrote certain excellent little works, in which he exercised his talent splendidly. Of these the following, written in elegant meter, are reported: Life of Saint Trudo: one book. Life of Saint Bavo: one book. Life of Saint Remold: one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

    Peter Alphonsus, converted from Judaism to the faith, previously called Moses, whom King Alphonsus, raising him from the sacred font, distinguished with his own surname, a man in wri-

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 54

    learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy. As proof of his sincere faith, under the name of Moses, the Jew that he had been, and of Peter, the Christian that he began to be, he wrote a distinguished dialogue, Against the Jews, one book, “To the one and eternal First.” On Knowledge and Philosophy, one book, and certain other works. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

    Honorius of Autun, priest and scholastic of the church, a man most devoted to the Scriptures and very learned, and nobly instructed in the secular sciences, subtle in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote many excellent little works. Of these he himself, in the book On Illustrious Men, which he entitled On the Luminaries of the Church, listed the following: a very necessary work on Christ, on the Church, and on the future life, which he entitled Elucidarium, three books, “You say that you wonder why.” On Free Will, one book. The Seal of Saint Mary, one book. The Mirror of the Church, or Of Sermons, one book. A Stumbling Block concerning Priests, one book. A Summary of Histories, one book. Gem of the Soul, on the divine offices, six books, “A battle-line in the camps of the eternal king.” On the Image of the World, two books, “The world, therefore, is so called as if [unclear].” On the Song of Songs, one book, “At the beginnings of books there are three.” On the Luminaries of the Church, one book, “Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome.” On the Body of the Lord, one book. On the Hexaemeron, one book. On God and Eternal Life, one book. On the Soul, one book. The Ladder of Heaven, on the degrees of visions, one book. The Key of Physics, on the natures of things, one book. On the whole Psalter, one book. Homilies on the Gospels, one book. On the Pope and the Emperor, one book. A dialogue from the little works of Augustine, one book. Refreshment of Minds, on feasts, one book. The Food of Life, on the saints, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He also published many other works, whose titles I have not yet been able to find. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man from his youth most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and in secular letters second to none in his time in the territory of Liège, practiced in both verse and prose. He wrote many volumes in both styles, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Yet this is to be blamed in him: that, adhering to Emperor Henry, a rebel persecutor of the Roman Church, he wrote letters and little works against the most holy pope Gregory VII, which did not befit his profession. What he wrote, however, he declared openly at the end of Illustrious Men. When he was placed in the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz to instruct boys, he wrote in heroic meter: The Life of Saint Theodoric, Bishop, one book. The Passion of Saint Lucy, in meter, one book. On the Translation of the Same, one book. The Life of King Sigebert, one book.

    Book

    The Passion of the Thebans, in meter: one book. The Life of Saint Guibert: one book. The Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux: one book. The Life of Saint Maclou: one book. The Life of Saint Theodard: one book. Against Pope Gregory: one book. An Apology to the Emperor: one book. Against the Letter of Pope Paschal: one book. On Ecclesiastes, in heroic meter: one book. Histories after Eusebius: one book. On Illustrious Men: one book. On the Ecclesiastical Computus: one book. Also Sermons: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. After these he also published other works, which he did not mark with the above-written little works. He flourished in the times of Henry, the third emperor, the fourth king, in the year of the Lord 1110. He carried his Chronicle down to the year 1111.

    Calixtus, the second pope, a Burgundian by nation, brother of the duke of Burgundy, formerly archbishop of Vienne, sat in the pontificate after Gelasius for six years. He was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a particular lover of Saint James the Apostle, in whose honor he raised the church of Compostela to an archbishopric. He wrote, in a composed style and with the greatest diligence:

    On the Miracles of Saint James: one book. “Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants.” Letters to various persons: one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Stephanus, also called Herrandus, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Halberstadt, from being abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. He wrote some little works not unworthy of reading, but few have come into our hands. In the person of Count Louis he wrote a very elegant and useful letter to Waltram, bishop of the church of Nienburg, defending Henry, rebel against the Roman Church:

    A Defense of the Pope: one book. “As a good man from a good...” And several letters to various persons: one book. And certain other things. He died under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1107, in the fifteenth indiction, and was honorably buried in Reinsburg.

    Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian order, a Burgundian by nation, was a noble and holy man, who was renowned for many miracles in life and after death; learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters; subtle in intellect, adorned in speech, since indeed he neglected nothing in his writings that could contribute to the adornment of his discourse. He published many excellent little works, of which the following are reported:

    On Consideration, to Eugene: five books. “The thought comes to me to dictate something.” Of His Meditations: one book. “Many people know many things, but...” On Contempt of the World, to clerics: one book. “To hear, as we believe...” On Grace and Free Will: one book. “You asked me, brother Gotfrid...” To the Knights of the Temple: one book. “When I was speaking recently before...” The Mirror of the Religious Life: one book. “To Hugh, soldier of Christ...” On the Cloistered Ladder: one book. “If anyone among you to amend...” To the Carthusians: one book. “When on a certain day bodily...” To the brothers of Mont-Dieu in the east, Bernard

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 55

    On conscience: one book. On the order of life: one book. On the two eyes of the soul: one book. On the confession of sins: one book. On precept and dispensation: one book. To Henry of Sens: one book. To Hugh of Saint-Victor: one book. Against Gerard: one book. Against a heretic, to the pope: one book. On the misery of this life: one book. On temptations and leisure: one book. On the will: one book. An apology to the Cluniacs: one book. On the degrees of charity: one book. On the Passion of the Lord: one book. On the Magnificat: one book. On loving God: one book. On the psalm “He who dwells”: one book. On the Song of Songs, 86 homilies: one book. On “The angel was sent”: one book. To his sister, on the manner of living: one book. The Life of Bishop Malachy: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Several sermons: one book. And certain other works. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1111.

    Anselm of Laon, scholasticus, very devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice, and nobly learned in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished no less in life than in knowledge, explained the Scriptures of both Testaments in a new kind of exposition, with interlinear and marginal gloss from the writings of the Fathers. He also wrote certain other little works, which have not come to me. He is reported to have written:

    Commentaries on the Psalter: one book. And certain letters. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1110.

    Hugh, priest and monk of Saint-Victor at Paris, of the order of regular canons of Saint Augustine, abbot there, as they say, a Saxon by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, inferior to none of the ancients in secular philosophy, who was regarded in his time as a most celebrated teacher, like a second Augustine; subtle in intellect, adorned in eloquence, and venerable no less for his way of life than for his learning. He wrote many, almost innumerable, little works, of which few have thus far come into our hands:

    A Summa of his Sentences: twelve books. “Arduous indeed and laborious...” On the soul of Christ: six books. “The first of all things to be sought...” Didascalion: one book. “I shall speak secretly to my soul...” On the pledge of the soul: one book. “With what zeal, with what affection...” On the manner of praying: one book. “So many praisers now...” On the praise of charity: one book. “Because, brothers, by the Lord’s granting...” On the instruction of novices: one book.

    Book

    On the Rule of Saint Augustine: one book. On the mystical ark of Noah: one book. On Ecclesiastes, sixteen homilies: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On the Lamentations of Jeremiah: one book. On the hierarchies of Dionysius: fourteen books. On the praise of the fathers: one book. On the perpetual virginity of Saint Mary: one book. On the Magnificat: one book. On “Thou art all fair”: one book. On the love of the bridegroom and the bride: one book. On the medicine of the soul: one book. On meditation: one book. On the incarnation of the Word: one book. On the wisdom of Christ: one book. On the vanity of the world: one book. On the substance of love: one book. On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: one book. On discipline: one book. On the five books of Moses: one book. On the mysteries of the Church: one book. On spirit and soul: one book. On the Lord’s Prayer: one book. On confession: one book. On the prophet Ezekiel: one book. An epitome of philosophy: one book. On certain psalms: one book. On marriage and concupiscence: one book. On the simple nature of God: one book. On the threefold will in Christ: one book. On the power and will of God: one book. On Sacred Scripture: two books. On the nature of animals: one book. On contemplation: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. He also composed many sermons and other different and varied treatises. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1130.

    Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne Agrippina, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, with the Holy Spirit enlightening him through a vision, and not ignorant of secular letters, a monk of Saint Lawrence of Liege, was taken thence on account of his incredible learning by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and elevated as abbot of the monastery of Deutz. He composed many excellent little works. For from the time when in his youth he entered the monastery, he had exercised himself so greatly in the Holy Scriptures that not even while sleeping did he seem able to rest from meditating on them, but his tongue and lips moved as though he were reading. Of his little works I have at present found only the following. To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg and afterwards bishop of Regensburg:

    On the victory of the Word of God: thirteen books. On Genesis: nine books. On the Song of Songs: six books. On the book of Saint Job: ten books. “These precepts which under...” “When once I was sitting in the community...” “Those things which from the book of Solomon...” “At the beginning of our labor...” “Where he sits,” etc., as to the letter. “The Jews seek signs, the Greeks...” “Man, the microcosm, that is...” “Meditation is frequent...” “There were certain men who...” “You ask about the soul:” “O unclean world,” etc. “Because it was said to me that I should think...” “There are seven petitions.” “Alone, solitude,” etc. “You ask about the will.” “You ask about power.” “The reader of the divine Scriptures...” “The lion, strongest of beasts...” “The spiritual [unclear] of the Lord,” etc. “Recently, when you, a welcome guest...” “Whoever of the faithful soul, while...” “He who against [unclear] his son for himself...”

    10

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 56

    On the books of Kings, concerning David: 15 books. On the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament: 42 books. On the Apocalypse of John: 12 books. “That you also, venerable [unclear].” On the divine offices: 12 books. “Those things which through the cycle of the year are arranged...” Meditations on the fire of [Tuicium?]: 3 books. “Behold, because the accuser Satan...” On the twelve minor prophets: 30 books. On the Gospel of Matthew: 8 books. On the Gospel of John: 13 books. On the Rule of Saint Benedict: 1 book. An Apologetic for the same work: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book.

    Finally, it is said that he wrote many other things too, and explained the New and Old Testament for the greater part in many books; of these up to the present we have seen nothing except the works which we have marked. He flourished in great holiness, shining with doctrine and miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1124. And he died under Lothar III.

    B[ertus?], abbot of the monastery of Limburg in the diocese of Speyer, of the holy order, magnificently learned, distinguished in life and conduct, so that he deserved to be visited by frequent divine revelations. For many years he devoted himself in the school of Paris to secular philosophy, and became a noble philosopher. But, considering the passing nature of the present life, he abandoned the pursuit of vanity and, returning to his homeland, became a monk in the said monastery and finally was made abbot. He wrote, however, little works not contemptible for reading; of these I have found only the following:

    On the Song of Songs: 4 books. “Whoever of himself and of things...” On contempt of the world: 2 books. “The world is called by an improper name...” On Saint John the Baptist: 1 book. “The historian of the Gospel relates...” Of his revelations: 1 book. “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1124...”

    He wrote certain sermons on the saints whose bodies or patronages were held in the same monastery of Limburg. He flourished under the emperor Henry V, with no small reputation for holiness, in the year of the Lord 1124.

    Rudolf, abbot of Saint-Trond in the diocese of Liège, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man practiced with constant zeal in the divine Scriptures, and not meanly learned in secular letters; strong in verse and prose, an excellent musician, and no less renowned in work than in knowledge. He wrote in both styles little works not to be despised, of which they report:

    Against the simoniacs: 7 books. Also a Chronicle: 1 book. Many poems.

    He also composed many chants in praise of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1125.

    Hranco, second abbot of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed in secular doctrine, strong in talent and renowned for eloquence. He wrote certain commendable little works, both in meter and prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. While he was still a simple monk in the aforesaid monastery, at the command of Fulgentius his abbot he began a small work, which afterward, when made abbot, he completed, adorned with knowledge and eloquence:

    On the grace of God: 1 book. On the state of future glory, in meter: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book. Sermons on the blessed Virgin: 1 book. And certain other things.

    BOOK

    He was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Hafligem under the emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1109, in the thirteenth indiction.

    Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, formerly a scholastic of Paris, surnamed Porreta, by nation a Frenchman, a man much practiced in the divine Scriptures and splendidly learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and confused in speech by the novelty of his terms, was accused by blessed Bernard of heresy in certain points; and, convicted in the council of Rheims celebrated by Eugenius, he is said to have renounced the error. There are those who excuse him, saying that the authorities introduced in his expositions were understood by some in a less than sound way. But we, agreeing with the Roman Church, confess that what has once been determined by it may be infringed by no one. Gilbert wrote many little works, of which they report the following:

    On the whole Psalter, one book. On all the epistles of Paul, fourteen books. On the Gospel of John, one book. On Boethius, On the Trinity, one book. Books of Questions, etc. Several sermons, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Conrad III, in the year 1140.

    Ivo, abbot of Mount Saint Cornelius, of the order of the divine father Benedict, learned in the holy Scriptures by continual practice, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters for his station, endowed with a noble talent for expounding the divine volumes, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing various treatises. But I do not remember that any of them has come into our hands. His notable work to Milo, bishop of the church of Terouanne, likewise a most learned man, is said not yet to have been seen:

    On the Song of Songs, one book. Several sermons and letters. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Lothar, the last emperor, in the year 1130.

    Gilbert, bishop of Chartres, studious and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and inferior to none of the doctors of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, sharp in intellect and sufficiently adorned in eloquence, distinguished in morals and life, and an especial lover and worshipper of the most blessed Mary, mother of God, wrote a notable little work on this prophecy: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah.”

    Against the Jews, one book. On the Nativity of Saint Mary, one sermon, of approved custom. Various sermons, one book. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge. I believe that he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

    Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly instructed in the letters of the humanities, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, notably distinguished, after the manner of the ancients, in composing and declaiming homilies to the people. He wrote, in dialogue form, the disputation that he had had with a certain Jew on the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the first letter of his own name and that of the Jew disputing with him being noted:

    To Wilbodo the monk, one book. On the Canon of the Mass, one book. “There was a certain rich man.” On the steward of iniquity, one book. And he composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

    Edmund, a monk of Canterbury in England, of the order of Saint Benedict, formerly a hearer and disciple of Archbishop Anselm, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long practice, and [unclear] of secular letters, made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant one volume on the discord that existed between William, king of the English, and the aforesaid Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury:

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 57

    On ecclesiastical liberty: one book. The Life of the same Anselm: one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Gratian, a monk of Bologna or Classe, of the Order of Saint Benedict, by birth, as some maintain, an Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and burning with admirable zeal, ready in intellect and clear in eloquence, also distinguished in life and conduct, wrote, after Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a notable volume of Decrees from the statutes, enactments, and writings of the ancients, which professors of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is: The Concordance of Discordant Canons: four books. The human race by two... He also composed certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Hugh, monk of Corbie, of the Order of Saint Benedict, called de Fouilloy, a man rich and learned in the Holy Scriptures through reading the ancients, distinguished in intellect and sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable for conduct than for knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote a notable volume, not so much useful as delightful to all religious persons and those fearing God, divided into four little books, designated beforehand as follows: On the material cloister: one book. On the arrangement of the cloister. On the spiritual cloister: one book. The contemplation of the soul’s cloister... On the cloister of the soul: one book. Into the heavenly [unclear] cloister. On the cloister of paradise: one book. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Richard, monk of Saint Victor in Paris, of the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, outstanding in morals and conduct, wrote many and almost innumerable little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported: On the Holy Trinity: five books. My righteous one lives by faith. On contemplation: one book. Arise, Lord, into your rest. On the twelve patriarchs: one book. Benjamin, a little youth. On the mystical ark: five books. That mystical ark of Moses. On the Song of Songs: one book. On my bed, etc.; the soul which God... On the extermination of evil: one book. What is it to you, sea, that you fled? On the promotion of good: one book. Every head is sick, etc. Against the Judaizers: one book. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, etc. On the tabernacle of the covenant: one book. Whatever you shall bind upon... On the forty-two stations: one book. In the regeneration, when he shall sit... On the study of wisdom: one book. Since to your question, etc. On the perfection of monks: one book. Bring to the Lord, sons of God, etc. On mental prayer: one book. Those things in the Gospel. On the threefold holocaust: one book. On the authority of Peter: one book. On judicial power: one book. On the difference of sins: one book. On the instruction of novices: one book. On the spirit of blasphemy: one book.

    Book

    On the offices of the Church, one book. On diverse affections, one book. An epitome of the whole Bible, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. On Daniel the prophet, one book. A chronicle from the beginning of the world, one book. On the double Pascha, one book. Of divisions or exceptions, twenty-four books. “O God, supremely good, unchanging.” On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar, one book. On the sacrifice of Abraham, one book. On the four winds, one book. On the words of Isaiah, one book. On the words of the Apostle, one book. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On violent charity, one book. On newness of life, one book. “Purge out the old leaven.” He also composed, besides these, many letters, sermons, and various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Guigo, fifth prior of the Charterhouse, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long study, and not ignorant of secular letters either, mild in talent and distinguished in speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in learning, is said to have composed several little works, by which his name was given to immortality. Among these there is extant an excellent work, in lucid style, On the Life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, one book, written [unclear]; On the Institutes of the Carthusians, one book; and certain other things. He corrected with diligent study, according to the line of truth, the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, corrupted by the excessive fault of copyists. He died under the younger emperor Lothair, in the year of the Lord 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

    Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris after being a scholastic, a man most devoted to the divine writings, nobly learned, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, transmitted his name by writing to posterity with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians everywhere, exercised in his little works, names and holds him as Master with singular veneration. For with sagacious study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work: Sentences, three books. “Desiring something from.” On the whole Psalter, one book. “Since all the prophecies the Holy Spirit.” On all the letters of Paul, fourteen books. “The beginnings of things must be sought.” Various sermons, one book. He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Eckard, first abbot of the monastery of Saint Laurence which is called Aura, in the diocese of Würzburg, in the Bircinian Forest, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, among the Germans in his time, inferior to none of the learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he displayed the liveliness of his intellect. Of these I have seen only an excellent work, put together in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled: The Lantern of Monks, five books. He composed certain elegant sermons and various letters to different persons. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130. In the middle

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 58: buried in the church of the aforesaid monastery.

    Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, distinguished in talent and speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in learning, made his name known by writing and expounding various works, and both by word and by example did things by no means insignificant for the edification of his brothers. For he wrote:

    Elegant sermons, one book. On Vices and Virtues, one book.

    He also published several other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

    Peter, priest of the church of Troyes, surnamed Comestor or Manducator, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently taught in secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, wrote certain distinguished little works in both styles, whose authority has long since been approved by the Church through usage. He was called Comestor or Manducator because, by citing the authorities of the Scriptures rather frequently in his sermons and little works, he seemed, as it were, to have eaten them into [the belly?] of his memory. Among the other volumes of his talent he wrote a notable work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, briefly and usefully explaining all the historical books of the Bible, which from usage is now entitled:

    The Scholastic History, twenty books. “Of imperial majesty is ...”

    In Praise of Saint Mary, one book. Sermons on the season, one book.

    Sermons on the saints, one book. And very many other things. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    Peter the Parisian dialectician, called Abelard, French by nation, a man most learned in secular philosophy and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, delighting in novelty of terms and attempting to search into things too high for him, overcome by glory, fell into several errors. Through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, he was condemned together with his depraved doctrines in the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote several little works, which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have been of use to posterity. Of these there exists a volume shadowed over with dialectical obscurity, varied in many opinions, which he wished to entitle:

    His Theology, one book. Know Thyself, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Adelphus, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long practice, not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a useful shepherd to the sheep of Christ committed to him, is said to have fashioned several little works for their benefit, in which a rich vein of talent recommends ornate speech. Of these there exist elegant works:

    Sermons to the brothers, one book. Against the Saracens, one book. The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

    William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, afterward, as is said, a monk of Clairvaux under the blessed father Bernard of the Cistercian Order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also distinguished by holiness of life and conduct, for that reason especially beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading. Of these few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, forestalled by death, did not finish:

    The Life of Saint Bernard the Abbot, one book. “About to write the life of your servant ...”

    The Mirror of Faith, one book. The Enigma of Faith, one book. Sentences of Faith, one book. To Theophilus, On the Nature of the Soul, one book.

    Book

    On Contemplating God, one book.

    On the Nature and Dignity of Love, one book.

    On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

    Meditations for Novices, one book.

    Against Peter Abelard, one book.

    On the Song of Songs, incomplete, one book.

    On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book.

    And certain other things. There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that widely known letter to the Carthusians, whose beginning is: “To the brothers of Mont-Dieu, an eastern light ...”; it is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140. And after he had completed one book on the life of Bernard himself, he died; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

    Conrad, monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, [unclear] musician and distinguished poet, composed many splendid little works under the name Peregrinus; in these, the ornate arrangement of thought and the cultivation of graceful discourse show their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge. A notable work of dialogues under the name of Peregrinus the priest and Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled:

    The Mirror of Virgins: 8 books. “As I am about to confer with you, O Theodore...” On the Gospels [unclear]: 1 book. “Since in the letter of the Old Testament...” On his life and the fruit of death: 1 book. “Since every discourse of the divine page...” On the matricularii: 1 book. “Since it is manifest to the world...” On the Praises of St. Benedict, in verse: 1 book. “Like light from the sun of virtues...” Didascalon: 1 book. “Since I see that you have long been at leisure...” On music and tones: 1 book. “Music is [unclear] of a certain [unclear]...” Of the rest I have seen nothing. There was another declaimer of the Order of Preachers, who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons for the people under the name Peregrinus, much inferior to ours in eloquence and later than he in time. But whatever Conrad wrote in this way echoes Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not do.

    He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once a very close friend of the blessed abbot Bernard, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular writings, ready in talent and clear in eloquence, and no less distinguished in conduct than in doctrine, made his name known to posterity by writing. For when William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, died and left unfinished the work on the life of Saint Bernard, and when that saint himself also was already holding the heavenly realms, Arnold wrote and completed:

    Life of Saint Bernard: 4 books. “The deeds of illustrious men do not...”

    And some letters. He flourished under Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    Richard, monk of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, by everyone’s report, most learned in secular letters in his time, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, who, by writing and composing various treatises, transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. I do not recall that any of them have so far come into my hands. Yet his notable and famous work is reported:

    Histories of the Times: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book.

    He flourished in the times of Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    Anfredus of Auxerre, monk of the Cistercian order, once a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard, but, lest he should also become an imitator of his error, betook himself to the instruction of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; under his discipleship, distinguished in doctrine and religion, he composed little works of reading not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity:

    Against Peter Abelard: 1 book. On the Apocalypse of John: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book.

    He flourished in the times of Frederick I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers Fol. 59

    Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and among all the teachers of his time most learned in the sacred letters, a notable grammarian and philosopher, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen his notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled Aurora, as follows:

    On Genesis: 1 book. “In the beginning, the world and what things in the beginning...” On Exodus: 1 book. “These twelve first [unclear]...” On Leviticus: 1 book. “But the voice of the Lord [to] Moses...” On Numbers: 1 book. “God addresses Moses and...” On Deuteronomy: 1 book. “These are the words of God by which...” On Joshua: 1 book. “After Moses, Joshua [unclear] the people...” On Judges: 1 book. “The Hebrew sins, says the Scripture...” On Ruth: 1 book. “Peter’s style hastens to Ruth...” On Kings: 3 books. “Dwelling on Mount Ephraim...” On the Song of Songs: 1 book. “Origen alone, with the learned...” On the Fourth Book of Kings: 1 book. “King Solomon reigned...” On Daniel: 1 book. “[unclear] the king, subjects to himself...” On Tobit: 1 book. “Whoever reads the history of Tobit...” On Job: 2 books. “Some attribute the book of Job to Moses...” On the Book of Judith: 1 book. “Eustochium, favoring Paula...” On the Book of Esther: 1 book. “All the way to the Ethiopians, who...” On the Books of Maccabees: 1 book. “Great Alexander, who...” On the Gospel History: 1 book. “Herod shone with the right of kings...” On the Acts of the Apostles: 1 book. “In the nineteenth year of Tiberius’ reign...” Recapitulations: 1 book. “These things concerning the new and old law...” On Grammar: 1 book.

    He published many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. In the aforesaid little works he expounded the historical books of the Bible with marvelous brevity, and, carefully observing the law of meter, he explained each item in its historical and allegorical sense.

    Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the Order of Saint Benedict, originally from Calabria: a man studious and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, since he was regarded in his time as a prophet, also attempted to predict future events. But it would seem to me, speaking without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, that he spoke more from conjectures drawn from Scripture than prophetically. For, to pass over the rest for the moment, he dreamed that the emperor Frederick III would be a future enemy of the Church; yet we all know that, right up to his death, he remained peaceful, subject to the Roman pontiff and faithful. He wrote a number of little works in clear language, in almost all of which he was accustomed to mingle, as if future and foreclosed, [unclear].

    On Jeremiah the prophet: 1 book. On Daniel the prophet: 1 book. On the Gospel of John: 1 book. On the Apocalypse of John: 8 books. To Henry VI: 1 book. “You piously ask that something be explained.” On the Seven Seals: 1 book. “The first synagogical time.” The Psalter of Ten Strings: 2 books. The Book of Concord: [unclear] book(s). On the Fifteen Pontiffs: [unclear] book(s). On Future Times: [unclear] book(s). Letters to various persons: [unclear] book(s).

    He also published many other works, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.” He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

    Rui, of the fathers of Benedict, a Frenchman by nationality, a man practiced by constant study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular disciplines, distinguished in talent and clear in eloquence, wrote several little works of his own genius, by which his name became known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable History of the deeds done in the Holy Land by Christians in the time of Urban II against the infidels: [unclear] book(s). “Among all the historiographers.”

    I have seen nothing of the others. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

    Osuida, a noble woman born in Saxony, a nun in the monastery of Gandersheim, which is not far from Hildesheim, was distinguished by wondrous talent and learning. For the sacred virgins, exhorting them to chastity and continence, she wrote in Latin:

    Six comedies. “The one hope of the world,” etc. A panegyric on the deeds of the Ottos, in hexameter verse. Also the Passion of Saint Dionysius in elegiac verse. Also, on Saint Gangolf and other saints, several works.

    She also had knowledge of the Greek language. She was a contemporary of John the Englishman, who by her learning deserved the papacy.

    Dudechinus, priest of the church in Langenstein, a German by nationality, a man learned in the holy Scriptures through long practice and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, for the hope of eternal reward set out with many others under the emperor Conrad III for Jerusalem. In frequent naval battles with the Saracens, he shone forth with great devotion and constancy for the faith of Christ. After he returned to his homeland, at the request of Cuno, abbot of Mount Saint Disibod, then of our order, he wrote, in sufficiently elegant discourse and in the form of an epistle or little book, the History of that same pilgrimage: [unclear] book(s). Letters to various persons: [unclear] book(s). And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Rupert, bishop of Lincoln, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most skilled of all the learned men of his time; a philosopher, astronomer, and notable calculator; easily the foremost theologian of his time; subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, transmitted his name with glory to posterity by writing many and various works. Of his little works few have come into our hands. The following, however, are reported:

    Summa of Theology: [unclear] book(s). On the Books of Dionysius: [unclear] book(s). A Summa which is called Numerical: [unclear] book(s). On the Celestial Sphere: [unclear] book(s). On Ecclesiastical Computation: [unclear] book(s). A beautiful Calendar: [unclear] book(s).

    He published many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

    John, bishop of Chartres, a native of Salisbury, formerly clerk and disciple of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury: a man learned in the divine writings, nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, composed with fair grace, excellent in verse and prose, and no less religious

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 60

    nor venerable in learning. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read the distinguished work On the Trifles of Courtiers and Philosophers, which he wished to entitle Polycraticon, in eight books, “Most delightful, then, in many things.” Penitential, one book, “Since the mercies of the Lord are.” Life of Saint Thomas the Archbishop, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

    Petrus Blesensis, archdeacon of Bath, the close friend of the aforesaid bishop Iohannes Carnotensis, to whom he dictated some letters, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also exceptionally learned in secular letters; acute and forceful in talent, he knew how not to flatter the vices of princes and prelates, but to rebuke them. On account of his learning and the integrity of his life he was held in esteem among kings, princes, and bishops. He wrote many little works, among which these are reported: On Christian Friendship, one book, “Because true things have been diminished.” On Salutary Penance, one book, “You asked me that I might [write] something for you.” On Hastening the Passage, one book, “Who will give water to my head?” On the Quality of Penance, one book, “The excessive austerity of your severity.” “You are divided and your heart.” Against the Depraver, one book, “Your little exhortation.” Letters, 184 in number, in two books, “Most urgently elected, reverend father.” And On the Office of a Bishop, one book, “As often as I recall the words.” On the Danger of Prelates, one book, “I give thanks to your grace, since.” On the Life of Clerics of the Court, one book, “Asked by you, bishop.” Letters of Fortune, two books. He also wrote many other things. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    Alexander, the third pope, a Sienese by origin, after Adrian IV sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years. He was a learned and energetic man, who endured many injuries from the emperor Frederick; while he resolutely crushed the three antipopes raised up by him against himself, and at last overcame the emperor himself. As a sign of his subjection, he trampled his neck with his foot, saying: “It is written: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” He wrote elegant letters to various persons, one book; and On Ecclesiastical Power, one book; and certain other things. He died in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1181, in the fourteenth indiction.

    Crisolanus, archbishop of the church of Milan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, produced certain works of great authority, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. None of these has come into our hands. There is reported to be his Against the Greeks [unclear], one book; On the Holy Trinity, one book; letters, sermons, and other various treatises, which are unknown to me.

    Hugo Eterianus, a Tuscan by nation, easily the most learned in the Scriptures among all learned men of his time, and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a most eloquent philosopher and rhetorician, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin speech, whom all Greece admired as he wrote, most subtle in talent and second to none as a disputant. He wrote many excellent volumes both in Greek and in Latin, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only a certain work, brief indeed, but not to be despised, on the heresies which the Greeks heap upon the Latins, addressed to Cardinal Ardoinus, one book, “Your diligent prudence.” On the Immortal God, one book.

    Book

    Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

    He flourished in the times of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with whom he was of great authority, under Frederick, the first Roman Augustus, and Pope Alexander IV, in the year of the Lord 1160.

    Christianus, archchancellor of Frederick, the first emperor, German by nation, a man most learned in secular literature, eloquent and industrious, whom the Italians admired when he spoke in his own time, also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, whom Leo the Tuscan, notary of Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, extols with praises. He wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, of which there are extant:

    The Deeds and Life of Frederick, the first emperor.

    Of Various Letters, one book.

    Certain Speeches, and other things.

    He flourished under the same Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1170.

    Leo, Tuscan by nation, chief interpreter of the imperial letters under Manuel, prince of the Greeks, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent cultivator of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech. His office was to translate letters sent to the emperor, or to be sent to others, from one language into another. He published certain excellent volumes, and also transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read only the distinguished work which he entitled:

    On the Transgressions of the Greeks, two books: The intolerable [unclear] of the Greeks.

    Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book.

    He flourished at Constantinople in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1170.

    John, archdeacon of a certain church of Horit[unclear], a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain little works, not to be despised, for the edification of the faithful, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a distinguished and excellent work addressed to Stephen, a certain royal notary, against the Greeks:

    On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, one book: Many things of the Greeks in rounded [unclear].

    Also various letters.

    But he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come into our hands.

    Odefridus of Viterbo, priest, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, distinguished, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there is extant a large volume addressed to Pope Urban III, in verse mixed with prose composition, on the beginning of the world, on the whole Old and New Testament, on the ages of the world, the times, deeds, and all histories, which he entitled:

    Pantheon, eighteen books: On the beginning of the world.

    Concerning the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, and Henry his son, in the year of the Lord 1185.

    Eckebertus, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florin, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, was the brother of the blessed virgin Heliçabet, abbess of Schönau. He had formerly been a canon of the church of Bonn; called by his holy sister to Schönau, he first became a monk, and then was made abbot. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these I have found the following:

    Against Heresies, one book: The prophets had long ago [unclear] times.

    On the Beginning of the Gospel of John, one book: The mysteries of the divine word.

    On the Magnificat, one book: The Spirit of the Lord is upon you, Mary.

    On “The Angel Was Sent,” one book: The Gospel sermon [unclear].

    For Virgins Consecrated to God.

    On the Death of His Sister, one book: A word is to me for you, O king.

    Meditations, one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 61

    Sermons through the year, one book: “There shall be signs,” etc., the Advent of the Lord.

    Praises of the Savior, one book. For he was a distinguished declaimer--

    Letters to various persons, one book. --an outstanding declaimer, learned and eloquent, so much so that in a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one could refute.

    He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an outstanding declaimer, learned and eloquent, so much so that in a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one could refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Florinus, which is called Schonau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year 1160, and on account of his religion and learning he was held in esteem.

    Elizabeth, nun and abbess of the sisters of the monastery of Schonau of the Order of Saint Benedict--for there are two monasteries, one of monks, the other of nuns, situated at the edge of the diocese of Trier, not far from the Rhine, in the Hircinian forest--sister of the above-mentioned Abbot Eckbert, was a virgin of most holy conduct, who had received many revelations from God and committed them to writing for the edification of posterity. Of these I have read the following:

    The Way of God, a useful work, one book: “It happened at the beginning of the fifth.”

    On the Eleven Thousand Virgins of Cologne, one book: “To you who [have] pious affections.”

    Various Revelations, one book: “All who are going to read.”

    To her brother Eckbert, one book: “You ask me, brother, for this.”
