    Johannes Gluel, German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Cologne, sprung from Aachen, an imperial city, a man outstandingly learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his study, a volume not to be rejected by the cultivators of this religion, on the origin and progress of his order, which he entitled: Mirror of the Carmelites, one book. Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book, [incipit:] “Lay up [unclear].” Lenten Sermons, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. He flourished in his convent at Cologne, writing and composing various little works, where at last, when his strength failed, he ended his day and was buried in peace.

    Heinricus Euta, or Oyta, German by nation, the unique ornament and co-founder from the beginning of the University of Vienna in Austria, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, of which very few have so far come into our hands. For I have read only: On the Sentences, four books, [incipit:] “Concerning the prologue of the first [book] of the Sentences [unclear].” On Contracts, one book, [incipit:] “Love justice, you who judge.” On the Conception of Saint Mary, [incipit:] “A virgin shall arise from Israel.” And certain sermons. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the University of Vienna under Emperor Wenceslaus, together with Heinricus de Hassia, in the year of the Lord 1390.

    Heinricus de Andernacho, German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent, famous among all men of his time as a declaimer of sermons, published little works of authority not to be lightly esteemed; of these the following are reported. A distinguished work:

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 98

    On the Sentences: four books. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Questions of philosophy: one book.

    And certain other works which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He flourished especially in the convent at Cologne, where he is said to have been buried.

    Lasius Andernarius, a Gaul by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, nobly exercised in the arena of scholastic discipline, distinguished in talent, an outstanding disputant. He wrote some notable volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following distinguished, splendid work excels:

    On the Sentences: four books. Questions and Collations: one book.

    He is also said to have written some works on moral philosophy, but they have not come to me.

    Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, jurist, the most celebrated of all in his time, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, whose sayings are held in great authority among professors of civil law. He published certain splendid little works on laws, by which he consecrated the memory of his name to immortality among posterity. Of these the following are reported:

    On the Code: nine books. On the Institutes: four books. On the Use of Fiefs: one book.

    And many others. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and of Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

    Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, an outstanding doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, polished in eloquence, distinguished no less for religious conduct than for knowledge of letters. He wrote certain notable little works for the instruction of monks. Of these the following are extant. A work which he entitled:

    On the Eating of Meat: one book. Explanations on the Rule: one book. Questions on the Sentences: one book.

    Besides these, he is said to have written various and numerous treatises; but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands, except that little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which he beautifully sets out and rightly concludes that, for a healthy monk professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the eating of meat is illicit and therefore wholly forbidden.

    Richardus Lauinham, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man excellently learned in the holy Scriptures, an eminent interpreter of secular philosophy, and also of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He also wrote some volumes, of which these are reported:

    Against the Lollards: one book. On the Foundation of His Order: one book. For the Book of Bridget: one book. Various Sermons: one book. Also On Logic: one book. And Various Questions: one book.

    He flourished in the University of Oxford, especially at the time when the heresy of John Wycliffe and of the Lollards began in Bohemia.

    Johannes de Werdena, of the order, as they report, of the Friars Minor, a Teuton by nation, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, rich in the reading of the ancients, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy, in talent

    excellent; composed in speech with scholastic simplicity; in his time a very celebrated preacher of popular sermons. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote very useful little works necessary for preachers of the word of God, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

    Sermons on the Temporale, in two sets: book. Sermons on the Saints, in two sets: book. Sermons also for Lent: book. But the other things which he composed have by no means come to our knowledge. Let us put on, etc. We see [unclear].

    Jacobus, who is called the Great, by country a Toledan, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished for his knowledge of natural philosophy, and rich in reading of the ancients. He is said to have issued various treatises and commentaries on the divine books, which have not yet come into our hands. I found one excellent, notable volume of his, entitled On the discourse of the inquiry of wisdom:

    Sophilogium: book.

    Of the others I have seen nothing.

    Of the most illustrious prince.

    He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

    Johannes Campscen[us?], of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, long exercised in the holy Scriptures by study, rich in talent through continual reading of the ancients, an excellent preacher of sermons. He is said to have forged certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these, the following are reported to be extant and very notable:

    Sermons on the Temporale: book. Sermons on the Saints: book.

    But I could not find the titles of the other works which he composed.

    Thomas Gualensis, of the order of the Friars Preachers, an Englishman by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very studious, and also nobly learned in secular letters, especially in scholastic philosophy; subtle in talent, clear in eloquence; likewise an excellent preacher of sermons, an acute disputant in scholastic lectures. He wrote many distinguished little works on the holy Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Yet of these few have come into our hands. For I found only the following:

    On the whole Psalter: book. On the Proverbs of Solomon: book. On Augustine’s City of God: book. On the Song of Songs: book.

    He flourished in the University of Oxford, where he is said to have composed many volumes, especially various lectures on several books of the Bible.

    Philippus, abbot of the monastery of Otterburg, in the diocese of Worms, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned by long exercise, not ignorant of secular literature. For the edification of readers he issued volumes not to be despised; by them, exercising his talent properly, he also left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these the following are reported. A distinguished, notable work:

    Sermons on the Temporale: book. Sermons on the Saints: book. Book of letters to various persons.

    If he issued anything further, it has as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

    Nicolaus, a physician of exceptional learning, an Italian by nation, by country a Florentine, a man most learned not only in medicine but also in the other letters of secular philosophy, clear in talent, elegant in eloquence; how great his learning may be among physicians

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 99 ... of this time is confirmed not by my words but by their testimonies. He published certain distinguished little works in that faculty. Among these there is said to be an excellent work: Summa medicinae, one book; and certain others.

    He died in the time of Rupert, king of the Romans, and Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1412, indiction 5.

    Johannes de Duren, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, German by nation, a man studious in the Holy Scriptures and nobly practiced in them, of great and distinguished reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have fashioned certain little works for the guidance of simple priest-preachers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive: Sermones de tempore, one book; Sermones de sanctis, one book; Quadragesimale, one book, “Sanctificate the fast ...”; “When a suitable confessor ...”; De septem peccatis mortalibus, one book, “There is a way which seems right to a man”; De occultis vitiis, one book; De confessione, one book.

    He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

    Hilmannus de Hachenberg, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, having a polished tongue through practice in speaking; in delivering sermons to the people he shone forth as a very great and most renowned man. He wrote certain little works, not to be despised by simple persons, by which, fruitfully applying his talent, he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive: Sermones de tempore, one book, “There shall be signs ... he foretold”; Sermones de sanctis, one book; Sermones per quadragesimam, one book.

    And certain others.

    He flourished in his convent at Koblenz, where he died and was buried.

    Johannes de Lignano, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, outstanding in talent, renowned for eloquence. He is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works in canon law; by applying himself to these he spent his time usefully and also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, as Franciscus de Zabarellis testifies in the prologue on the Clementines, there survive compilations: Super Clementinis, one book; and certain others.

    He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1405.

    [Hugo?] de Sletstadt, German by nation, a man studious and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, subtle in talent and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions. He wrote certain, as they say, distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survives: Quaestiones sententiarum, three books, a work [unclear]; and certain others. He was, moreover, in his determinations, a follower of the Order of Friars Minor of the holy father Bonaventure, a clear interpreter, explaining those things which in that man’s singular philosophy could have seemed obscure and rather uncommon to simple persons.

    Paulus Venetus, of the Order of Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in Aristotelian philosophy, second to none in Italy in his time; subtle in talent, scholastic, and an excellent declaimer. He composed many little works, especially in philosophy, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these they report:

    BOOK.

    Against the Jews: 1 book. ["Bound by [the testimonies] of very many…"] A Summa on natural [philosophy]: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. Sermons for Lent: 1 book. On the [books of] Posterior [Analytics]: 3 books. ["All doctrine, etc."] On the Physics: 8 books. ["By natural philosophy…"] On the Metaphysics: 12 books. ["With you, most wise…"] On [the books] On the Soul: 3 books. ["So great [a study] of letters, etc."] A Summa of philosophy: 3 books. ["A colloquy below, etc."] A twofold Logic: 3 books. ["Completing the rest…"] On [the book] On Generation [and] Corruption: 3 books. ["Of human and divine [things]…"] On the [book] of Porphyry: 1 book. ["Greatest, to the strong, etc."] On the book of the Categories: 1 book. ["To me, seeking, etc."] On the Consequences of Strode: 1 book. ["[I take] Jesus, God [and] man…"] And several others. He flourished under Wenceslaus the emperor, in the year of the Lord 1400. And, dying young, he was buried in the sacristy of his order at Venice.

    James of Thessalonica, of the order of Friars Preachers, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, excelling in talent, polished and composed in speech, second to none of his time in declaiming sermons to the people. He published certain illustrious volumes, by which he left to posterity a praiseworthy memory of his name. Of these there is extant a notable work, entitled "On the morals of men and the offices of the noble and of the common people," setting forth [its] subject: On the game of chess: 3 books. ["Among all kinds of signs…"] Various sermons: 1 book. But the others which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

    Thomas de Haselbach, a Teuton by nation, erudite in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, scholastic in speech, but too diffuse [and] prolix, and on that account liable to the reproach of certain [persons]. For when he was the ordinary lector of sacred theology in the gymnasium of Vienna, reading for twenty-one years on the prophet Isaiah, he did not reach the end of the first chapter. He wrote some little works on the divine Scriptures, of which the following are reported—many volumes: On Isaiah the prophet: 1 book. ["After [that], by God's gift, in such wise as…"] On the Sentences: 3 books. On the Ten Precepts: 1 book. On the five senses of man: 1 book. Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. But the others which he is said to have written have by no means come to our knowledge.

    Thomasinus, of Ferrara by country, of the order of Friars Preachers of Saint Dominic, a man studious [and] learned in the holy Scriptures, a distinguished declaimer in correcting the sins of peoples. He is reported to have forged certain illustrious little works for the instruction of simple priests, by which he transmitted to posterity the notice of his name with praise. Of whose number these are foremost reported: Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. Sermons for Lent: 1 book. But the rest which he composed have not come to our knowledge hitherto. He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Gregory XII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    [The source here repeats the Thomasinus of Ferrara entry verbatim; not re-translated.]

    On Ecclesiastical Writers Folio 100

    Thomas de Kempis, a German by nation, a canon of the order of Saint Augustine, of the Mount of the holy martyr and virgin Agnes near Zwolle in the diocese of Utrecht, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an especial lover of blessed Mary ever virgin. He wrote little works, not to be despised, for the instruction of simple brothers. Among them the following are reported:

    On contempt of the world, three books, “He who follows me shall not.” Sermons to novices, two books, “Behold how good and pleasant.” Sermons to the brothers, one book, “He who has not renounced.” Dialogue of novices, one book, “I ask you, dearest father.” On the solitary life, one book, “Dearest, since you were in.” On the three tabernacles, one book, “It is written in the prophet.” On true compunction, one book, “Weep with me, all you friends.” The little garden of roses, one book, “With the holy you will be holy.” The valley of lilies, one book, “I am the flower of the field and the lily.” The alphabet of a monk, one book, “Show me your ways, Lord.” Consolation of the poor, one book, “Be comforted, be comforted.” The epitaph of a monk, one book, “The way of the just has been made straight.” What a monk ought to be like, one book, “Listen, religious monk.” Manual for beginners, one book, “Let the little children come.” Instructional book for youths, one book, “Son, from your youth receive.” Another work on contempt of the world, one book, “The Lord rules me, and nothing.” Letters to various persons, one book, “Dearest brother, gladly.” And certain other works.

    He flourished in the times of Rupert, Bavarian king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Nicolaus, monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross in Austria, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and rich in the reading of the ancients, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote certain useful little works, not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his talent to posterity. Among them the following are reported: a work not to be despised in praise of the most blessed mother of God and virgin Mary, useful to preachers, which he entitled:

    The Image of Saint Mary, two books, “The name of the virgin Mary: Lu.” Various sermons, one book.

    The rest, though many works which he composed are reported, have by no means come down to us.

    Bartholomaeus of Urbino, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a diligent investigator of the works of the holy fathers. He wrote volumes not to be despised, among which the following are reported. From the little works of Saints Ambrose and Augustine he gathered into one work, with singular zeal, according to the order of the alphabet, and gave it the title:

    The Milleloquium of Augustine, one book. The Milleloquium of Ambrose, one book. Also, On Spiritual Warfare, one book. And very many others.

    He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope Gregory XII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Franciscus de Platea, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and notably learned both in law and in secular philosophy, excellent in talent and an outstanding preacher of sermons, is said to have composed many splendid little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: an outstanding and splendid work which he entitled:

    On Restitutions, one book, “Whether restitution is of necessity.”

    Book

    On censures, five books. Various sermons, one book.

    The other works that he composed have not come to our knowledge by reading.

    Petrus de Candia, Cretan by nation, of the order of the Friars Minor, first bishop of Novara, then archbishop of Milan, afterwards cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff named Alexander V, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and splendidly learned in scholastic philosophy, a very celebrated preacher of sermons, who once presided over a public school in the university of Paris, and by teaching and writing gained great and immense praises. Among his most elegant little works there survive clear and useful commentaries:

    On the Sentences, seven books. Various sermons, one book. And certain other works.

    He died in the last year of Rupert, king of the Romans, and was buried in the convent of the Friars Minor at Bologna, in the year of the Lord 1410, in the third indiction.

    Franciscus de Bachone, a Catalan by homeland, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Girona, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular philosophy, had such strength in teaching and disputing in the university of Paris that he was surnamed the Sublime Doctor. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a great and notable work from the writings of the saints, widely useful to preachers of sermons to the people, which we may entitle:

    A repertory for preachers: 1 book. Also, On the Sentences: 7 books. It is reported besides that he wrote certain other things as well, but they have not come into our hands.

    Michael Berbrant of Düren, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a German by nation, lecturer in sacred theology and prior of the convent of Kreuznach in the diocese of Mainz, a learned man and so distinguished a preacher that, summoned not only in the neighborhood but also to distant places and cathedral churches, he preached to the admiration of all. He was in great familiarity and authority with John, the last count of Sponheim, and obtained many benefits from him for his convent. Among other things he wrote elegant works:

    Sermons on the season: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. Synodal conferences: 1 book. And certain other things.

    He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Petrus of Speyer, of the Order of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and splendidly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and famous for eloquence, very highly regarded in public opinion for preaching sermons to the people. He wrote certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these are reported:

    Sermons on the season: 1 book. Sermons on the saints: 1 book. On the books of the Ethics: 7 books. But the other things that he composed have not yet come to our knowledge by reading.

    Einardus of Fronthoven, a German by nation, of the Order, as they report, of the Friars Preachers, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled in them by long practice, and not ignorant of secular literature. He wrote works not without usefulness for preachers of the word of God, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have seen only:

    Sermons on the season: 1 book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 101

    Sermons on the saints: book [unclear]. Of other works I have seen nothing. He flourished, as his own people say, in the convent at Koblenz, where he died.

    Johannes Capreolus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, by homeland a Toulousain, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, excellently taught in the disciplines of Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect, quite capable in disputation, a most vigorous champion and defender of the sayings of Saint Thomas Aquinas. He wrote very distinguished monuments of his talent, by which he made his name known. Of these many volumes are extant:

    On the Sentences: 3 books. And various sermons: 1 book. And certain other things.

    He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1415.

    Henricus de Coesfeldia, by nation a German, of the Carthusian Order, prior of the house of Saint Mary near the Mount of Saint Gertrude in Holland, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, of great reputation, subtle in intellect, clear in speech, and also a very celebrated preacher of sermons. He wrote many excellent volumes, whose frequent use is judged useful for devout brothers, lovers of their own salvation. Among them the following are reported:

    On Exodus, mystically: 1 book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: 1 book. On the three substantial vows: 2 books. “Do not love the world.” Against the vice of ownership: 1 book. On the three monastic guardianships: 1 book. On the instruction of novices: 1 book. The Mystical Circumcisorium: 1 book. On the sacrament of the altar: 1 book. On the Lord’s Annunciation: 1 book. Eulogium of Paul the Hermit: 1 book. Sermons on the season: 1 book. Letters to various persons: 1 book. And very many other things.

    The difficult work of William of Paris, bishop, On the Whole Corporeal, Incorporeal, or Spiritual Universe, he traversed with wonderful industry and beautifully enclosed in a brief compendium. He died in the house of the Valley of Grace near Bruges, beneficially occupied in the act of visitation, in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1312, indiction 3, on the sixth day before the Ides of July.

    Henricus Hachenburg, of the Order of Friars Preachers, by nation a German, a man magnificently practiced and well instructed in the divine Scriptures, of excellent talent and very celebrated reputation in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote volumes not to be rejected for the direction of simple priests. Of these there are extant:

    Sermons on the season: 1 book. “I will come and heal him.” Sermons on the saints: 1 book.

    He flourished, as his own people report, in the convent at Koblenz, where he composed various works.

    Jordanus, of the Order of the Friars of Saint Augustine of the Hermitage, by nation a German, a devout man, an excellent expounder and interpreter of the divine Scriptures, of most excellent talent in preaching sermons. He wrote several elegant treatises useful to devout brothers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Yet few of these have come into our hands. The following, however, are reported:

    On the Apocalypse of John: 1 book. Apology of his order: 1 book. On the Passion of the Lord: 1 book. “Look and make according to the example” [unclear].

    Book

    Sermons on the temporal cycle: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Lenten sermons: one book. Various questions: one book. And many other things. "Behold, he will give voice to his voice." He flourished under King Rupert, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Petrus, bishop of Nova Civitas, an Italian by birth from the town of Bruniquelli, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in ability and renowned in eloquence. He published several little works of great usefulness, by which, with magnificently exercised talent, he entrusted his memory to posterity. Of these, the following are reported. A certain notable work in which he reduces all the histories of the New and Old Testament to alphabetical order, and arranged them under individual topics:

    On the Sentences: four books. On the Proverbs of Solomon: one book. Also on Ecclesiastes: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. And many other things.

    Moreover, he is said to have adorned almost the whole Bible with excellent commentaries. He flourished under Rupert, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Laurentius Justinianus, a Venetian by birth, of the Celestine Order, and afterwards patriarch of Venice, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in the conduct of his life; although he could have possessed the greatest riches and honors of this world, scorning all things for the love of Christ, he entered the aforesaid order. In it, shining with great religion and abstinence, he published very devout little works for the edification of the simple, whose titles are reported below:

    The Tree of Life: one book. On Monastic Discipline: one book. On the Marriage of the Word and the Soul: one book. On the Agony of Christ: one book. On the Interior Conflict: one book. On the Lamentation of the Church: one book. On the Sacrament of the Altar: one book. On the Solitary Life: one book. On Contempt of the World: one book. On the Lord's Discourse at Supper: one book. On the Pastoral Office: one book. Also on Obedience: one book. On the Degrees of Perfection: one book. Forty sermons: one book.

    He flourished in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410. He was buried at Venice in the cathedral church. At his tomb many miracles are divinely performed. His life was clearly described by Bernardus Justinianus, his nephew.

    Augustinus of Rome, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, prior general, a man very devoted to and deeply learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly educated in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability and renowned in eloquence, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survive:

    On the Sentences: four books. On all the epistles of Paul: fourteen books. On the Apocalypse of John: one book. On Free Will: one book. On Original Sin: one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 102

    On Christ and the Church: one book. On the charity of Christ toward the elect: one book. On the perfect righteousness of the Church: one book. On the power of the pope: one book. On the books of the Ethics: eight books. He is said besides to have written many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of Pope John XXIII, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Baldus Perusinus, once a hearer and disciple of Bartolus of Sassoferrato, the most celebrated jurisconsult of all his time, and also nobly learned in secular philosophy, acute in talent, profound in judgment, cautious and firm in counsel, wrote many distinguished little works in both laws, by which he secured for his name eternal remembrance among posterity. Of these number the following are reported:

    On the Code: nine books. On the Old Digest: twenty-four books. On the New Digest: twelve books. On the Infortiatum: thirteen books. On the Institutes: four books. On the use of fiefs: one book. On the Authenticae: one book. On the second book of the Decretals: one book. Additions to the Speculum: one book. Many counsels: one book. And many other things.

    He died in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1423, in the first indiction, and was buried with honor at Pavia in the convent of the friars of Saint Francis, in the month of July.

    Angelus Perusinus, brother of the above-mentioned Baldus, and his companion and associate in studies, most learned in civil law, distinguished in talent, and most celebrated in fame and reputation among jurisconsults, also composed many volumes in his faculty; by establishing in them monuments of an excellent intellect, he destined the memory of his name for the knowledge of many. Of these number the most elegant commentaries are reported:

    On the Code: nine books. On the Old Digest: twenty-four books. On the New Digest: twelve books. On the Infortiatum: thirteen books. On the Institutes: four books.

    Indeed, on the whole body of civil law; and he is said to have labored over certain other things. He died in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the same year as his brother Baldus, in the year of the Lord 1423, in the first indiction.

    Petrus de [Ancharano?], Italian by nation, Bolognese by homeland, once a hearer of Baldus Perusinus, a man most skilled in both laws and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy; although he was bound by the bond of a wife and occupied with family affairs, nevertheless, always engaged in the study of letters, he published many little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these number are reported:

    On the Decretals: five books. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals: one book. On the Clementines: one book. On the rules of law: fourteen books. On the Old Digest: thirteen books. On the New Digest: twelve books.

    Book one book. Several counsels: [unclear] book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1410, the co-father of Franciscus de Zabarellis.

    Incentius Gruner, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, brilliant in intellect, scholastic in speech, published little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there survives a notable lecture, which he publicly wrote and read before the students at the new foundation of the Leipzig academy: On the office of the Mass, three books, To the honor of the blessed... Disputed questions, one book. And certain other things. He flourished at the time of the transfer of the University of Prague to Leipzig, into the province of the Margraviate of Meissen; Alexander V, pope, confirmed it and endowed it with privileges, in the year of the Lord 1410.

    Johannes de Aurbach, German by nation, priest of the church of Bamberg, a man zealously learned in the divine Scriptures, brilliant in intellect, scholastic in speech, published little works of authority not to be dismissed, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only a distinguished work: On the sacraments of the Church, one book, To the praise of God and the salvation of souls... Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished in the city of Bamberg and wrote various little works.

    Dionysius de Burgo Sancti Sepulcri, of the order of the Hermit Friars of the divine father Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote little works not to be scorned in each literature, by which he left perpetual monuments of his intellect to posterity. Of these the following are reported: very beautiful and elegant commentaries: On Valerius Maximus, one book. On the Metamorphoses, [unclear] book. On the works of Virgil, [unclear] book. On the tragedies of Seneca, [unclear] book. On the Politics, [unclear] book. On the Rhetoric, [unclear] book. And certain other things. Moreover he reduced all the fables to a pleasing tropological sense. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1412.

    Petrus de Aliaco, bishop of Cambrai and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, once chancellor of the Paris academy, teacher of Johannes de Gerson, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, especially in Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in intellect, brilliant in speech, and also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name and intellect. Of these I have found the following: On the Sentences, four books, What doctrine is this... On the praise of Holy Scripture, one book, Upon this rock build... On the beginning of Mark, one book, What doctrine is this... On the stability of the Church, two books, Whether the Church of Peter by law... The mirror of consideration, three books, Whoever from the trouble of the world... A compendium of contemplation, three books, Since many wise men... On the spiritual ladder, one book, There are four spiritual... Briefly on the Psalter, one book, A shortened word he made... Meditations on Psalm 70, one book, O Lord my God, it terrifies me...

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 103

    On laws and sects, one book. On a general council, one book. An exposition of Psalm 70, one book. Meditations on Psalm 42, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the seven penitential psalms, one book. On the Lord's Prayer, one book. On the same, anagogically, one book. On the Ave Maria, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. On the Canticle of Zachariah, one book. On the Canticle of Simeon, one book. On the election of a pope, one book. On spiritual exercise, one book. On the twelve honors of St. Joseph, one book. On the soul and its accidents, one book. A harmony of theology and astronomy, one book. On the sacraments of the Church, one book. Various sermons, one book. Several letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things.

    He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, at which he was also personally present, in the year of the Lord 1416.

    Nicholas of Clémanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, having obtained the mastership of the sacred page in the university of Paris, gave great proof of his learning. He wrote, in both styles, many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of his most brilliant talent. Of these, the following are reported. To lord Peter of Ailly, bishop of Cambrai, the aforementioned cardinal, he wrote a distinguished work which he entitled:

    On the fruit of the desert, one book. On the corrupt state of the Church, one book. On new feast-days, one book. On the matter of the schism, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And many other things.

    He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1417.

    Johannes Dominici, cardinal of the title of St. Sixtus, commonly called Ragusan, a Florentine by homeland, of the Order of Friars Preachers, who was sent by Pope Gregory XII to the Council of Constance on behalf of union, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

    On Ecclesiastes, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Magnificat, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. Entitled Lucula noctis, one book. An itinerary of devotion, one book. On the love of charity, one book. If I speak with the tongues of men.

    Book

    Sermons on the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. Sermons through Lent: one book. Blessed is the man who has not gone away. And certain other works.

    He died at the Council of Constance, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418, in the eleventh indiction.

    John, bishop of Lombariensis, German by nation, Basel by homeland, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and renowned for eloquence, a most celebrated preacher of sermons, published some little works of no contemptible reading, by which he handed down the memory of his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these, the principal are reported to be:

    On the Sentences: four books. Various sermons: one book. And certain other works.

    He is said besides to have delivered many orations and conferences to the clergy, and also before the supreme pontiff and the assembly of cardinals, which I have not seen.

    John Zacharias, German by nation, Erfurt by homeland, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, also an excellent interpreter of secular philosophy, subtle in talent and a very acute disputant, very capable in delivering sermons both to the clergy and to the people, wrote certain excellent little works by which he made his name known. Of these are reported:

    On the Sentences: four books. On Genesis: one book. On Exodus: one book. On Leviticus: one book. On the Epistles of Paul: fourteen books. Various sermons: one book. And certain other works.

    He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, and at the Council of Constance he was magnificently praised for disputing against heretics, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Antonius de Butrio, Italian by nation, Bologna by homeland, easily the most celebrated jurist of all in his time, and exceptionally learned in other writings, both divine and human, renowned in talent and eloquence, and no less venerable for honorable conduct than for learning, published little works on the laws, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

    On the Decretals: five books. On the Clementines: one book. A repertory of canon law: one book. A repertory of civil law: one book. Most elegant counsels: one book. And certain other works.

    He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of the general Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord [1427?].

    Gabriel of Spoleto, of the order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent and an outstanding preacher of sermons, wrote several commendable little works, by which he showed the knowledge of his lively talent also to posterity. But I have not hitherto deserved to see any of them. Yet the chief works of his are reported to be:

    Against the heretics: one book. Against the Fraticelli: one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 104

    And certain other things.

    He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

    Franciscus de Zabarellis, by nation a Paduan, cardinal priest of the Church, a man very learned in canon law, and nobly instructed both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote in law some works not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

    On the Decretals, one book, “Nothing new is [unclear].” On the Clementines, one book, “About to repeat the decretal.” On the canonical hours, one book. Various repetitions. And many other things.

    He flourished at the Council of Constance, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418. There also he died, buried among the Friars Minor. In his praise Poggio delivered an oration.

    Petrus Maurocenus, a Venetian patrician, cardinal bishop of the most holy Roman Church, a man very learned in divine Scripture and canon law, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, composed in speech, distinguished in life and conduct. He is said to have fashioned many excellent works, in which the liveliness of his intellect is recognized to shine forth. But I, up to the present, have not deserved to see any of them. There is reported of his an outstanding volume:

    On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. And various determinations.

    He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

    Nicolaus Dinckelspule, by nation a German, glory and rector of the Viennese university in Austria, very learned in the holy Scriptures, much instructed in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, notable in life and conduct, wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Among these the following are reported:

    On the Sentences, three books. Questions on the Sentences, one book. On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, one book. On the Ten Commandments, one book, “He writes on Matthew 22, q.” On the Lord’s Prayer, one book, “If you shall ask the Father anything.” On the eight beatitudes, one book, “In the Gospel which is read.” On the three parts of penance, one book, “It should be noted that, as the master says.” On the eight capital vices, one book, “There are two commandments of charity.” On the seven mortal sins, one book, “Consequently it must be said.” On the precept of charity, one book. On the sins of the tongue, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Moral sermons, one book. And many other things.

    He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, sent by the University of Vienna, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Petrus de Rosenhem, monk of the monastery of Melk in Austria, of the order of Saint Benedict, by nation a German, a man studiously learned in divine Scripture and magnificently instructed in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher and poet

    [unclear], prompt and distinguished in talent, published little works, not to be rejected, both in verse and in prose, in which he exercised his talent well. Of these there survives a metrical work which he wrote, at the persuasion and request of Nicholas Dinkelsbühl, to the lord Branda, cardinal of Saint Clement, apostolic legate in Austria, on the chapters of the whole Bible, which he entitled:

    The Rosy Memorial of Divine Things, one book. A Notable History of Times, one book. Various Sermons, one book. “Star-ruling one, heaven, earth.”

    He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420, and composed many and various works.

    Raphael Fulgosius, a Piacenzan by nation, a man most learned in both laws and well instructed in the precepts of secular philosophy, excellent in talent, cautious and steady in counsel, published certain distinguished volumes in civil law, by which he showed the force and liveliness of his talent also to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

    On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books. On the New Digest, twelve books. Many Counsels, one book. And certain other works.

    He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

    Johannes de Palomar, archdeacon of the church of Barcelona, an eminent doctor of decrees, nobly learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, published little works not unworthy of reading, through which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives an eminent treatise addressed to John, abbot of the monastery of the Scots of the order of Saint Benedict at Vienna:

    On Abstinence from Meats, one book. “The sons of Rechab shall rise in judgment.” Sermons and Questions.

    The other things that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. [The source scan here carries a second, degraded OCR capture of the Raphael Fulgosius works-list and floruit, double-captured into the Palomar entry; not re-rendered. See ERRATA, 2026-07-10.]

    Johannes de Teneramuda, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Sillimacus in Savoy, a man studious in the divine scriptures and very learned, devout in life and conduct, distinguished in talent, composed in speech, published little works very useful for the edification of religious brothers; by these he instructed not only those then present, but also those who would come after him, in the love of God. And they are these:

    On the Knowledge of God, one book. On the Nature and Fall of Man, one book. On the Restoration of the Fallen, one book. On the Love of God, one book. On the Joy of Man, one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 105

    On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. On the Christian Faith, one book. On the Honor of God, one book. On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book.

    He also elegantly composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

    Asparinus, a very celebrated grammarian, a native of Bergamo, born from the little village of Barzizza, a man most learned in secular letters, a philosopher and a most outstanding rhetorician, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, who raised the elegance of the Latin tongue, half-dead, from the underworld. He wrote many distinguished little works in that faculty, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive:

    On Orthography, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. Various Orations, one book. On the Letters of Cicero, one book. On the same author, On Duties, one book. On the same author, On the Orator, one book. On him, On Old Age, one book.

    I rejoice very greatly and [unclear].

    And certain other things. He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance, and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Antonius of Genoa, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine scriptures, a professor of canon law, a most celebrated interpreter, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to posterity. But I have not deserved to see any of them, except that which is entitled:

    A compendium of moral figures, one book. To religious men in Christ.

    The rest have not come to me.

    He flourished in person at the general Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

    Johannes de Imola, a Bolognese by homeland, a very celebrated doctor of both laws, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, whose learning and eloquence splendidly illumined all Italy in his time, is said to have published many distinguished volumes in both laws, whose authority among professors of this faculty is raised up with the highest praises. Among these, the following especially are reported:

    On three books of the Decretals, three books.

    On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book.

    On the Clementines, one book.

    On the Digest Infortiatum, fourteen books. Before we come to...

    On the Digestum Novum.

    And certain other things.

    He died at Bologna in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1426, in the fourteenth indiction.

    Antonius of Parma, of the Camaldolese Order, prior general, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, composed in eloquence, and sufficiently fit for delivering sermons to the people, wrote several distinguished little works for the guidance of preachers of the word of God, by which he made his name known. Of these the principal ones are reported:

    Sermons for the Temporale, one book. When [unclear] time had drawn near.

    Sermons on the saints, one book.

    Sermons throughout Lent, one book.

    And certain other things.

    He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord

    in the year 1420.

    Leonardus Aretinus, an outstanding philosopher, orator, and historian, and a most learned man [unclear], skilled in Greek and Latin speech, was first secretary of the Roman pontiffs Innocent VII, Gregory XII, Alexander V, and John XXIII, up to the Council of Constance; and afterward, having been summoned by the Florentine senate, he was appointed general chancellor. In this office he remained until the end of his life with great fidelity and authority. Among other things he wrote:

    A notable work of Dialogues, 1 book A History of His Own Time, 1 book On the Deeds Well Performed by the Florentines, 12 books On the Praises of Florence, 1 book A History of the Goths, 3 books A History of the First Punic War, 2 books The Life of Aristotle, 1 book On the Life of Cicero, 1 book A volume of Letters, 1 book

    In addition he composed some other works with great elegance, which have not come to my knowledge. Besides this he translated many works from Greek into Latin, namely the treatise of the blessed priest Basil on the instruction of pupils; he also translated from Plutarch the lives of Tiberius and Gracchus [unclear], of Paulus Aemilius, of the younger Cato, and of Sertorius the Romans. He also translated the little book of Xenophon On the Tyrant, Plato's Gorgias and Phaedo, and certain letters; Aristotle's Economics and the books of the Ethics and Politics he translated [unclear]. And other things which have not come to me. He flourished personally at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420. He died, however, under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, indiction 7, on the seventh Ides of March, at about the sixty-fourth year of his age.

    Pogius Florentinus, a philosopher and eloquent rhetor, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin speech, for many years a most eloquent writer within the apostolic [unclear]. He is said to have composed some little works of excellent talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Laurentius Valla was a very sharp rival of this Pogius, and wrote various things against him. He himself published:

    On the Situation of the Region of India, 1 book Against Laurentius Valla, 2 books Letters to Various Persons, 1 book Various Orations, 1 book And many other things.

    He made Dionysius Siculus and many other Greek authors Latin. Besides this, at the Council of Constance he delivered very many funeral orations. The work of filth which he entitled Facetiae we have judged rightly to be rejected from this catalogue of illustrious men, since its reading offends the devout, harms the unwary, and infects the carnal. He flourished personally at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Laurentius Valla, a Roman patrician, by far the foremost of the grammarians of this age in precepts, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most excellent theologian, subtle in intellect, sharp and eloquent, preferring Latin eloquence to Greek, composed many things for its adornment, and was very skilled in Greek and Latin speech. He published little works not to be scorned in reading, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

    Elegantiae, 6 books On the Reciprocation of suum and suus, 1 book Many Letters, 1 book Also Against Quintilian, 12 books Dialectic, 1 book

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 106

    Panegyric on the True Good, three books: “As I was undertaking, Paul...” On Free Will, one book: “I should very much wish, [Garcia?] [unclear]...” Apology against Poggio, one book: “I hear that Poggio another...” Against Antonio da Rho, one book. And many other works.

    He translated into Latin Homer, Thucydides, and several others. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance, under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420. Of him someone says as follows: What did that most biting censor of the Latin language, Lorenzo Valla, beget for himself by his harsh and exacting reproof? What other praise, I ask, did he obtain after death than that, according to his merits, that fine epigram composed about him is read and proclaimed everywhere: “Now, after his death, Valla’s shades seek [unclear]; but he fears to be the censor of his own tongue.” What he thought about the Donation of Constantine, by which Constantine endowed the Roman Church, his pestilential book shows; would that so great a man had never published it.

    Johannes Tortellius, an Aretine by nation, very close friend of Lorenzo Valla, to whom he wrote the six books of the Elegances of the Latin Language; subdeacon and chamberlain of the Roman pontiff, and afterward companion of Pope Nicholas, the intimate associate of his studies; perfectly trained in Greek and Latin letters, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a great and distinguished volume, which he entitled:

    Commentaries on Grammar, one book: “The Greek letters by which...” Also on dialectic, one book. He published various letters, one book. And several other works.

    He translated into Latin the Life of Athanasius of Alexandria for Pope Eugenius; he rendered the historian Appian word for word. And other works. He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Hermannus Petra of Studorp, of the Carthusian order, a German by nation; a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct; vicar and rector of the house of nuns of his order, of Saint Anne near Bruges in Flanders, where for ninety years he flourished with much religious devotion and learning. He wrote certain devout little works of his talent, of which the following are reported: a notable work, divided into six volumes for the circle of the year, containing:

    Sermons on the temporal cycle, three books. Sermons on the saints, three books. On the Lord’s Prayer, 50 sermons, one book. On the governance of nuns, one book. And several other works.

    He died under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction.

    Omnibonus Leonicus, a man most learned in humane letters, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, the most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician of all in his time; once, at Venice, a hearer of Manuel Chrysoloras of Constantinople, who brought Greek letters back into Italy. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

    On Cicero’s Orator, three books: “How great Cicero’s Orator...” On the poet Lucan, one book: “In expounding this author...” On Quintilian, one book: “How much admiration...” On the praises of eloquence, one book. Many orations.

    And he published several other works, which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished under Si...

    under Emperor Sigismund: in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Heinricus of Hesse the Younger, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of [unclear] Mary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence. He published many very elegant volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name, and many of them he publicly lectured on in the universities before entering religion. Among these the following are reported:

    On the Sentences, three books. On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. A Dialogue between a bishop and a priest, one book. Useful Sermons, one book. And certain others.

    He died under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, in the sixth indiction.

    Johannes de Gerson, a Frenchman by nation, chancellor of Paris, formerly a disciple of Peter d’Ailly, cardinal of Cambrai; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, almost scholastic, sure and firm in judgment, cautious in counsel, and a very clear interpreter of doubts; distinguished in life and conduct, by far the foremost of the theologians of his time. He wrote, in verse and prose, many most excellent little works, by which his name will always obtain immortality among posterity; the reading of them is no less useful than pleasing to devout and religious men. Among these there are extant:

    On the Praise of Writers, one book: “To search the Scriptures.” On the Concordance of the Evangelists, one book: “That the Gospel has been spread abroad.” On Ecclesiastical Power, one book: “Ecclesiastical power ought.” On the Removability of the Bridegroom, one book: “But the days will come when.” On the Manner of Holding Faith in Schism, one book: “For removing certain.” On Ecclesiastical Unity, one book: “Ecclesiastical unity.” On Ecclesiastical Estates, one book: “Peace, which all.” On the Manner of Living of the Faithful, one book: “The first rule which.” On Ecclesiastical Defects, one book: “Perhaps the Church says to me.” On Schism, one book: “In the inquiry of truth.” On a General Council, one book: “About to give occasion.” A Trialogue on Schism, one book: “Very often the lofty.” On the Marriage of the Church, one book: “A marriage was made in Cana.” What Things Must Necessarily Be Believed, one book: “A concise declaration.” On Various Heresies, one book: “A protestation or revocation.” On Appeal from the Pope, one book: “It is asked whether this.” Against Peter de Luna, thirty articles, one book: “And first it is established, etc.” Against the same, Eight Articles, one book: “And first it must be noted.” On the Assumption and Humanity of Christ, one book: “To the reverend father in Christ.” Two Lectures on Mark, one book: “As it is written in.” On the Literal Sense of Scripture, one book: “But he who shall have blasphemed.” Against the Heresy of the Bohemians, one book: “Intending to offer, according to faith.” On the Testing of Spirits, one book: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.” On the Examination of Doctrines, one book: “Beware of false prophets.” A Trialogue against Astrology, one book: “The wisdom which is from the Lord God.” On True and False Visions, one book: “Recently one from the readings.” On the Superstitious Observance of Days, one book: “The apostle blames those who.”

    On spiritual poverty: one book. On the value of prayer: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On the Magnificat: one book. A poem on the same: one book. On the angelic hymn: one book. On the Song of Songs: one book. On the marriage of Wisdom: one book. On the twofold logic: one book. To the governors of boys: one book. Sermons in the Council of Constance: one book. Sermons to the clergy: one book. Sermons to the people: one book. A dialogue on any question: one book. Several letters to various persons: one book.

    In addition he published many other minor works, indeed, but very useful ones, of which no certain knowledge has come down to us. He flourished in person at the Council of Constance. There, laboring gloriously for the extirpation of heresies, at length, when it had been dissolved, he was deprived of home, homeland, kinsmen, friends, dignities, and his own possessions for the defense of truth; he was beset by many plots. Hence, compelled by necessity, fleeing to the city of Lyon, he died there after a few years under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1429, in the seventh indiction, in the sixty-sixth year of his age, on the fourth day before the Ides of July. He was buried there among the Celestines with honor.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 108

    The Rule of his order: one book. Sermons for the season: one book. Sermons on the saints: one book. And certain other works. Martin V confirmed this rule, newly compiled in thirty-two chapters. He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Dominicus de Sancto Geminiano, a most excellent jurisconsult, and nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other literature of secular disciplines, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain outstanding volumes in canon law, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is an outstanding and very celebrated work divided into two volumes: Since the first gloss without. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals: one book. And various declarations. But the other works which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

    Paulus de Sancta Maria, a Jew by birth, a Christian by faith, first bishop of Cartagena and afterward prelate of Burgos in Spain, arch-chancellor of the king of Castile and Leon, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures, very learned, master of sacred theology, converted to the Catholic faith in his mature age, advanced so much in life and doctrine that among all the doctors of Spain he had no equal in his time. He wrote to his son Alphonsus, dean of Compostela, doctor of laws, on the postils of Nicholas of Lyra: Notable Additions: two books. What do you wish for yourself, that you corrupt. The Scrutiny of the Scriptures: one book. Search the Scriptures. And certain other works. He flourished, and completed this Scrutiny of his, under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1433, in the twelfth indiction, in the eighty-first year of his age.

    Petrus Paulus Vergerius, by homeland a Justinopolitan, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, a most celebrated rhetorician, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech, [translated?] certain outstanding little works of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher teaching Greek letters at Venice, by which he left remembrance of himself to posterity. Among these there is an outstanding work containing, on the deeds of the lords of Carrara: A very fine History: one book. On Noble Manners: one book. In Praise of Saint Jerome: one book. And many other works. He flourished at the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1421.

    Mapheus Vegius, by homeland a man of Lodi, datary of Pope Martin V, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned, and most learned in secular letters, a most celebrated orator and poet, distinguished no less for conduct than for knowledge. Through his care and at his expense, the relics of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, were transferred from Ostia Tiberina to Rome and placed in a new chapel richly built by him, in which he himself is buried. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, certain outstanding volumes, among which there is a very celebrated work, necessary for all religious, composed with divine and human learning, addressed to certain sisters, which he entitled: On Perseverance: seven books. Since serious matters often, as happens. On the Penitential Psalms: one book. In Praise of Saint Monica: one book. The thirteenth book of the Aeneid, in heroic verse: one book. Many epigrams: one book. Many letters.

    Book [unclear]. And many other things.

    He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    Johannes Plaeth, a German by nation, an ornament and pillar of the University of Heidelberg, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly a doctor in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, in life and conduct, so far as the secular estate permits, an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, among other things, a great and distinguished volume, which he publicly read as an ordinary lecture in the aforesaid University of Heidelberg:

    On the first [book], chapter [unclear], of the Decretals, one book, “Venerable fathers and lords.” Against the Bohemians, one book, “As the wise man says.” Questions on the Sentences, one book. Many sermons. Various questions.

    And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    A Heidelberg man, learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, an acute disputant, an excellent declaimer of sermons, formerly chaplain and secretary of Ludwig, Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine, and often envoy in many difficult causes, wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among them they report the following:

    Against the Hussites, one book, “When lately in the year of the Lord 1421.” Against the Feymeri, one book, “The law of the Lord [unclear] outwardly mortal.” On Contracts, one book, “As in the forum of the soul, where [unclear].” An oration before the King of England, one book, “Glory to God in the highest.” An oration before the Duke of Savoy, one book. Several letters, “My word is to you, O father.” Various questions, one book. Diverse orations.

    He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    Raymundus Sebeide, a Spaniard by nation, a man notably zealous in the divine Scriptures, who by teaching and writing in the University of Toulouse gave great proof of his learning. He is said to have written many excellent little works; of these I have seen only a large volume which he had publicly read in the aforesaid university. At its beginning he promises many glorious things, concerning whose truth some applaud themselves as if experienced; he entitled it:

    On Creatures, or On Man, one book, “To the praise and glory of the Most Holy.” Disputed Questions, one book. The rest are unknown to me.

    He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    Franciscus Barbarus, a Venetian patrician, a disciple in Greek letters of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a famous philosopher, and a supreme orator in both languages. While still young he wrote certain little works not to be rejected in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant the work which he entitled:

    On Wifely Matters, one book.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, folio 109. Sixteen books of Letters to various persons, and certain other things.

    From Plutarch he translated into Latin, for Zacharias his brother, the Life of Aristides, and of Cato, and of many illustrious men; other similar things. He died in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Nicholas V, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the third indiction.

    Thomas Walden, of the order of the friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by birth, prior general of the English province, a man most learned in divine scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect, sufficiently fit for disputation, no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge, also an excellent declaimer of sermons, and formerly confessor and secretary of Henry V, king of the English, wrote, among the other monuments of his intellect, a notable work divided into three great volumes against the mad Wycliffite and Hussite heretics, which Pope Martin V, after it had been examined, confirmed by apostolic authority. This work is entitled:

    The Doctrinal of the Church, three books: “Let God arise, let them be scattered.”

    Also On the Sentences, four books.

    On the books of the Ethics, ten books.

    On the books of the Physics, eight books.

    On the books On the Heaven and the World, four books.

    On Generation and Corruption, two books.

    On the books of the Meteors, four books.

    On the books On the Soul, four books.

    He is said to have written many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He died at Rouen and was honorably buried in his own convent, under Emperor Sigismund, in the last year of Pope Martin V, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430, in the seventh indiction, on the third day of the month of November, that is, the third Nones.

    Paulus de Castro, the most celebrated jurist of all his time, a man of great learning and eloquence, who for many years taught civil law gloriously, having been engaged for a public salary at Siena, Florence, and Padua, composed many little works on the laws, known and dear to the professors of this faculty, by which he left to posterity the memory of his most celebrated name. Among these the following are reported:

    On the Code, nine books.

    On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

    On the New Digest, twelve books.

    On the Infortiatum of the Digest, fourteen books.

    On the Institutes, four books.

    Most elegant Counsels, one book.

    And several other things.

    He died in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1437, in the fifteenth indiction.

    Ambrosius Florentinus, general abbot of the Camaldolese order, once a hearer of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher teaching Greek letters at Venice, a man most learned both in divine scriptures and in secular studies, a most brilliant philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian, left to posterity many distinguished monuments of his intellect. He was nuncio and envoy of Pope Eugenius to the Council of Basel, where on his behalf he delivered a solemn oration to the fathers. He wrote a notable volume:

    Letters to various persons, one book.

    Various orations.

    And several other things. He also translated into Latin from Greek the four books of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, in a more elegant and easier style. Also the original Life of blessed John Chrysostom, for Emperor Sigismund. Likewise Basil On Virginity, for Cardinal Gabriel, afterwards Pope Eugenius IV. Likewise Laertius On the Lives of the Philosophers, for Cosimo de’ Medici. But three li-

    ... the books of St John Chrysostom to Stagirius, the possessed monk, he translated in clear and ornate language. And very many other works still unknown to us. He flourished in the times of the Councils of Constance and Basel, both of which he adorned by his presence, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    Aietanus, a native of Vicenza, a canon of Padua, a man devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and physician, a very celebrated theologian, who publicly taught sacred scholastic letters in the Paduan gymnasium and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote, as they report, several little works in both literatures, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these they report the following:

    On the books of the Physics, eight books. On the books On the Soul, three books. On the books On the Heavens and the World, three books. And very many other works. He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and of Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

    Heinricus Gulpen, abbot of the monastery of St Giles at Nuremberg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, German by nation, a distinguished jurist, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, and no less venerable for religious conduct than for knowledge of the Scriptures. Johannes Nider, in his little work On Ants, commends from experience the readiness of his intellect and the foresight of his counsel. He wrote elegantly on the seven distinctions:

    On Penance, one book. On Consecration, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. And certain other works. He flourished at the Council of Constance in person, when he was still a secular master of arts studying law, in the year of the Lord 1417.

    Jacobus Forliviensis, a philosopher and physician of very celebrated reputation, whom many declare to have far surpassed all professors of philosophy and medicine of his time, distinguished not only for learning but also for experience in curing human illnesses. He wrote, in his own faculty, very useful little works for those laboring in study, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these they report as the chief:

    On the Extension of the Degrees of Forms, one book. On the First Canon of Avicenna, one book. On the Aphorisms of the same, one book. Also on the Tegni, one book. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Sigismund, most Christian emperor, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430.

    Rudolphus de Buxella, from a village of Swabia, German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in the secular philosophy which they call Aristotelian, a distinguished professor of sacred theology, who acquired great praise for his learning in the Heidelberg gymnasium. He wrote in that faculty little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity, namely: Questions on the Sentences, one book; very useful sermons, one book; various questions, one book; many orations to the fathers, one book; And if holy mother Church. And many other works. He flourished in the Heidelberg gymnasium at the time of the Council of Basel and thereafter, in the year of the Lord 1420.

    Hugo of Siena, Italian by nation, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a renowned philosopher and very celebrated physician, of outstanding and excellent intellect. He wrote in medicine volumes for students not to be despised, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these they report:
