    Laurentius Bonincontrius, an eminent philosopher and astronomer, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, strong in verse and prose. He is said to have fashioned many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of many; but I have not yet been able to see any of them. There is said, however, to be an eminent work of his for the cycle of the year:

    Entitled Fasti: one book. And certain commentaries.

    Book

    And certain other works.

    He is still living in Italy, writing many and various things both in verse and in prose, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

    Johannes of Kaysersberg, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, who for many years has held the office of preacher in the cathedral church of Strasbourg. He has written some commendable little works, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. They report, however, that the following elegant works are his:

    Sermons to the People, one book. Various Addresses to the Clergy, one book. And certain other works.

    This man, at great expense and with long labor, collected the works of Johannes Gerson, many of which he brought to us from France; dividing them into three parts in a very fine order, and preparing a very useful table, he gave the whole to the press. He is still living in the German city of Strasbourg, and composes various works, under the most renowned Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493.

    Johannes Pico, an Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola and lord of Concordia, a man most devoted to every kind of good letters, and, as he was most noble by illustrious blood, so also by a truly divine talent; surrounded by a great retinue [unclear] of arts of every kind, with whom he exercises the arena of books and studies, Latin as well as Hebrew and Greek; worthy and most deserving, whose perfection the Muses [unclear]. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a very acute disputant. He has written in a most elegant style some works which the age will both approve and especially admire, since they have not unworthily made the memory of his name and glory everlasting. Of him there are extant the following, which have already appeared:

    Heptaplus on the Beginning of Genesis. Also Nine Hundred Philosophical Conclusions. Apology. Also On the Psalms, one book.

    And several other works which have not yet presented themselves to our sight. He is still living today among the Italians in the company of his more gifted young men, and he does not cease either to write loftier things or to benefit posterity, under Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year in which we write these things, 1493.

    Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a German by nation, from the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, an excellent doctor of imperial law, a most eloquent counselor of the most illustrious Count Eberhard of Württemberg, and at the same time of the utmost integrity in law and faith; a most skilled investigator of all the most ancient philosophies and literatures. He was always most expert in the three principal languages, namely Hebrew together with Chaldean, and likewise Greek and Latin. He was also especially distinguished in French and in his own more polished vernacular tongue; and most learned both in the secrets of the divine Scriptures and in secular books. Indeed, in every kind of learning he is foremost in this age, as one who for many years has most earnestly penetrated the secret mysteries of the Greeks and Hebrews. Worthy indeed to devote himself to books alone, and not also to the noisy public court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could offer us anyone equal to so great a man. He has written some works by which he has commended his memory to those now living and to posterity:

    A dialogue addressed to Dalberg, chamberlain of the Vangiones, in which he explains all the secret, wonder-working words of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy; he entitled it Capnion, or On the Wonder-Working Word. On Rhetorical Preliminary Exercises. On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language. A funeral oration on the death of Rudolf Agricola.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers. Fol. 134 [unclear].

    Also letters and scholastic orations, more than can be numbered. Of epigrams and elegies: one book. Also scholastic letters and orations, more than can be numbered.

    Moreover he translated many little works from Greek into Latin for our common benefit: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates; Nestorius the Heretic; the Confession of Cyprian; Proclus On the Blessed Virgin; some of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead; a dialogue of the same author On the Council of the Gods; the Monomachia from Homer’s Iliad, on the duel of Paris and Menelaus, in the German language, in verse; Epiphanius On the Life and Death of the Prophets; Maximus of Tyre, the Platonic philosopher, in the oration: If God Made Good Things, Whence Do Evils Come? He lives to this day, devoted to letters, under Maximilian the king, and under his own prince Eberhard of Württemberg, whose illustrious name that distinguished Capnion renders still more illustrious by his talent, in the year in which we write these things, 1494.

    Conradus Leontorius, commonly called von Leonberg, of German nation, a monk of the monastery of Maulbronn, of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular matters, a philosopher, an orator, and a poet not to be rejected, skilled, as they say, in the three principal languages, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote some little works in verse and prose, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a volume: Letters to various persons: one book. Various orations. Many poems. And certain other things. He lives to this day among the Cistercians, and steadily continues in study under Maximilian, most renowned king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1304, indiction 12.

    Conradus Celtis Protucius, of German nation, born from Franconia in Germany, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, a fluent orator, an outstanding astronomer and cosmographer, a laureate poet, also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, skilled in both languages, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, wrote certain very fine little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he once read the following to me. To Maximilian, most renowned king of the Romans, on both rhetorical works of Marcus Tullius Cicero: An epitome, that is, an abridgment: one book. “Who in an assembly something.” On the Praises of Eloquence: one book. “The Morini celebrate with eternal [unclear].” On the Art of Versifying: one book. “Most illustrious prince, having received.” On Composing Letters: one book. “A letter or [unclear] is [unclear].” On the Situation of Nuremberg: one book. “When recently, to relax my mind.” A Sarmatian journey: one book. “To which he gave the name [unclear].” Poems: three books. “As often the proof of learned men.” Of loves which according to the four hidden [unclear] are inscribed: three books. “To write the things fated for our [unclear].” A panegyric to the duke of Bavaria: one book. “To attempt Italian lyres.” On the Life of Saint Sebald: one poem. “Offspring of royal stock.” The situation of Germany: one book. “About to write Germany.” Various orations: one book. He published many most elegant letters to various persons in verse and prose, and various epigrams; in cosmography, of which he is very knowledgeable, he wrote various things, which we trust will hereafter come to light. He is still living, being thirty-five years of age, and will write various things, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

    Petrus Bonomus of Trieste, protonotary of the imperial court, a man most learned in the Latin language, in composing poems of every kind both very ready and very practiced, as one from whose storehouse the tuneful Muses pour forth, and for that reason of great name and most celebrated fame, wrote very many things in prose

    Book

    [unclear]: and in verse of various kinds. Of these the principal works are extant:

    Books of Epigrams.

    A tireless collection of Letters.

    Nor does he ever cease writing. He is still living under his king Maximilian, devoted to letters and cultivating his talent with liberal arts, in the year in which we write these things, 1493, indiction 12.

    Sebastianus Titio, otherwise Brant, of Strasbourg, German by nation, a distinguished professor of both laws, and excellently learned both in divine Scripture and in the other disciplines of secular literature, not moderately skilled in poetry, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, who by his learning and nightly studies wonderfully adorns Basel, the renowned city of Germany. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, certain little works of by no means contemptible reading, by which he made his name well known. Of these there are extant:

    On the titles of both laws, book 1: “Since it is difficult.”

    A Sapphic Rosary of the divine Mary: “Of the human stock.”

    Riddles in praise of the Virgin from the Old Testament: “What things equal.”

    He proves the virginal conception possible: “Come hither, O.”

    The amazement of Mary when the angel arrived: “What do you wish for yourself.”

    The angel’s salutation: “Sent from on high.”

    On the wondrous places of the blessed Virgin: “May your, O Virgin.”

    The virginal compassion: “Son of the Father.”

    Christ’s consolation to his mother: “Why do you groan, O.”

    On Christ’s blows: “Look upon what things I have endured.”

    On the ingratitude of those eating manna: “By lot under this.”

    In praise of Saint Sebastian: “Why should I attempt your.”

    Life of Saint Onuphrius: “With our verses, I pray.”

    In praise of Saint Valentine: “With praises, O prelate.”

    In praise of Saint Ivo: “The beginning of the song.”

    Life of Saint Bernard: “O would that for me.”

    In praise of the order of the Charterhouse: “By the spirit of the holy.”

    On contempt of the world: “You, whoever you will be.”

    Praises of blessed Christiana near Basel: “Afterwards, because by merits.”

    Against slanderous advocates: “The manners of advocates.”

    On the captivity of King Maximilian: “Hear, O kings.”

    Elegy on the death of Emperor Frederick: “A wondrous thing lately was.”

    To the divine King Maximilian: “What does it profit, renowned king.”

    Of various epigrams, book 1.

    Commendatory poems for various printed editions.

    Besides these, with wonderful art and talent he compiled, in the common and vernacular language, a little book which he called The Ship of Narragonia. In it he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censured the morals of men, and handed on certain salutary remedies to each person, that one would rightly call that work not the book of fools, but rather a divine satire. For I do not know whether anything more salutary for the uses of the present age, or more delightful, could be read. They say that he is striving greatly so that this same work may soon appear also in Latin, both in verse and in prose. He is still living at Basel, being 35 years of age, and printers make very great use of his work and industry in embellishing their books. For he writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans; since, being singularly diligent, he has composed several very charming poems about him and to him, even secret ones, as they say, in the year in which we write these things, 1493.

    Jacobus Wimphelingus of Sélestat, German by nation, priest of the church of Speyer, a man most learned in divine Scripture and excellently taught in secular

    On Ecclesiastical Writers. Fol. 135

    [unclear]: a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, orator, and most outstanding poet of all; first at Erfurt and then in the school at Heidelberg, publicly lecturing on philosophy and sacred Scripture, he acquired great renown for his learning. A man learned in every respect, he is subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling in both verse and prose. He wrote in both kinds some distinguished little works, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these the following are extant. To Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, he composed a very celebrated work, most elegantly in hexameter and pentameter verse, which he entitled On the Threefold Brightness:

    In Praise of the Divine Mary, one book. Precepts of Rhetoric, one book. Praises of the Church of Speyer, one book. On the Holy Spirit, an oration, one book. To the King of France, an oration, one book. On the Art of Poetry, one book. The Greatest Hope of Our [unclear]. I Do Not Know If Your [unclear], Theoderic. How [unclear] Expect. Now Eight Lustra to Be Enjoyed. Many poems of various kinds.

    He composed many elegant letters, both to me and to others, the number of which is uncertain. At the request of Ludwig, bishop of Speyer, he composed the office on the compassion of the blessed Mary ever virgin, which is solemnly performed every year throughout that same diocese. To this Jacobus we have already long since dedicated the book On the Luminaries, or Illustrious Men, of Germany. He lives, in manly age, being about forty-three years old, in the renowned city of Speyer; he writes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493.

    Baptista de Salis, of the Order of Friars Minor of the province of Genoa, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed both in each law and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, devout in life and conduct, outstanding in observance of regular discipline: he published certain little works necessary for the instruction of simple priests, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these there is extant a very useful summa on cases in the forum of conscience, which, after the author’s name, is called:

    The Baptistinian Summa, one book. And certain other works.

    He completed that same summa under Frederick, the third emperor, and he is still living while his son Maximilian holds the kingdom, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Engelhard Funck of Schwabach, an East Franconian, German by nation, a learned man skilled in every respect, a philosopher, distinguished orator and poet, not ignorant of divine Scripture and pontifical law, outstanding in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling in both verse and prose: he is said to have fashioned certain little works in both kinds of style, by which he made his name known. In elegiac verse:

    On the Praise of His Fatherland, one book. On a Ring Given to Him, one book. Several letters to various people. Various epigrams. And many other works.

    He is flourishing at Rome, as an agent or advocate of cases; he composes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1493.

    Johannes Langer of Bolkenhain, priest of Wroclaw, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling in both verse and prose, in life and conduct worthy of the priesthood: he wrote, in each kind of style, many distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant an outstanding work addressed to Georg von Stein, lord of Steinau, which he entitled

    BOOK. [unclear] On revenues and redemption: one book. Letters to various persons: one book. Many poems, and several other works. He is still living in Wroclaw and is writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Werner Rolevinck of Laer, German by nation, Westphalian by homeland, of the order of the Carthusians, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man most devoted to sacred Scripture and very learned, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, published many distinguished little works, by which he made himself useful to those present and memorable to those to come. Of these the following are extant: a great work on all the epistles of Paul, which he entitled: The Teaching of Paul: fourteen books. The teaching of Paul the apostle [unclear]. Also On the Life of Paul: seven books. As I was with Moses, so [unclear]. On the Value of Masses: one book. On the Rule of Princes: one book. Bundles of Times: one book. Generation [unclear]. Paradise of Conscience: one book. The Lord God took the man. Many sermons: one book, and several other works. I once saw in his cell some treatises, small indeed but numerous and useful, whose titles forgetfulness has now taken from my memory. He is still living in the Carthusian house at Cologne, advanced in age, and is writing various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Arnold Bostius, German by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, a man devoted to and learned in sacred Scripture, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, of whom several letters to me are extant, wrote in verse and prose many distinguished little works. Of these the following are extant: a notable volume written in verse and prose, in which he clearly shows the prerogative, origin, and progress of his order in view of Marian protection; for this reason it was agreed to entitle it: On the Patronage of Mary: one book. You asked, most distinguished man, whether [unclear]. On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians: one book. To the venerable among [unclear]. On the Illustrious Men of His Own Order: one book. Brother Arnold Bostius [unclear]. Against Vincent of Nieuwkasteel: one book. How long will you always be foolish [unclear]. Letters to various persons: one book. On the Four Last Things: one book. Various poems, and several other works. He is still living at Ghent, in manly age, and composes various works; and by his example and writings he [unclear] many to holy studies [unclear] letters to various persons, in the year of the Lord in which I wrote these things, 1494.

    Heinrich Euticus, an East Frank, an excellent professor of both branches of medicine, published many works, which he is preparing for posterity. Likewise, in a different and elegant character, a very beautiful little work of poems, which he entitled: Scommata, or witty, urbane jests of youths. Several little works in medicine. A satire against sophistical dialecticians, enemies of the study of humanity.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers • Fol. 136

    On the praises of the blessed Virgin: And many other things. He is still living, when we wrote this, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1493.

    [Utelwolfus?] de Lapide, a noble man, German by nation and a Swabian, a man of great talent and a vigorous emulator of Roman eloquence, and for that reason having obtained great honor with the Margrave of Brandenburg, wrote to Georgius de Lapide, his uncle, a very great lover of letters, one book: A very polished letter-collection. And other things by which he will bring forth great praise for Germany among the cultivators of the Roman tongue. He is still living today, under Maximilian, in the year in which this was written, 1493.

    Rodulphus Langius, German by nation, canon of the church of Münster in Westphalia, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, orator, and very celebrated poet, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works both in meter and in prose, by which he has spread his name far and wide with immense glory. Of these the following are extant. To Hermann Langius, dean of the same church: On the City of Jerusalem, two books: Most splendid once was the city. To the dean of Cologne, a book of poems, one book: Bright virtue and of the heavenly ones. On the Siege of the City of Neuss, one book. A poem On the Three Magi, one book. Several letters to various persons. Various poems also, and a great many other things. He is still living, a very old man, in the city of Münster, composing many things under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which these things were written, 1493.

    Sebastianus Murrho of Colmar, German by nation, priest and canon in Colmar, a man devoted and learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher, orator, poet, and cosmographer, most skilled in the three languages, Hebrew, [Greek?], and Latin, renowned for knowledge of laws and canons, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole quadrivium, wrote, among other things, to Jacobus Wimphelingus of Schlettstadt, whom we mentioned above, a brief but very beautiful Epitome on the Praises of the Germans, one book. On the works of Baptista Mantuanus, one book. Several letters to various persons, and certain other things. He lives today in Colmar, where he is a canon, and writes various things which we hope will be published day by day, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493.

    Carolus Fernandus, German by nation, born at the town of Bruges in Flanders, deprived of sight from early childhood and for that reason utterly ignorant even of the elements, offers so great a marvel of himself that, like another Homer, he has become a poet, musician, [unclear], and very celebrated orator; also a most penetrating interpreter of the divine Scriptures, excelling in verse and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in expression, most upright in life and conduct. Having been granted a public and perpetual stipend by the king of the French, he taught humane letters excellently for a long time in the very celebrated school of Paris, and expounded a good many authors most beautifully. Finally, having despised all things, he abandoned the world together with his stipends; almost two years ago he entered the order of our holy father Benedict, in a properly reformed monastery which he calls Casale Benedictum, situated in a certain very dense forest about ten miles distant from the city of Bourges,

    in which he has persevered down to the present day, burning with great zeal for souls, so that, having been ordained deacon by apostolic dispensation, he publicly preaches the word of God with the greatest profit and admiration of all. He wrote many distinguished volumes, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity: On the metrical contest of Robert Gaguin concerning the most pure conception of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, against Vincent de Castronovo of the Order of Preachers, a most elegant work, Commentaries, one book, “We do not doubt from the Apostle.” Praises of the Order of Carmelites, one book, “While the Parthian turns his weapons.” Odes in praise of Christ, three books, “How much you surpass created things.” On the Conception against Vincent, one book. An iambic poem on the same, one book. An oration on the Conception to [unclear], one book. Many letters, two books. Almost innumerable poems, one book. Elegies on contempt of the world, one book. And many other things. He is living today, blind but very learned, composing many and varied works in the aforesaid monastery, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, indiction 12.

    Johannes Fernandus, brother of the aforesaid Carolus, himself a German by birth, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, a very celebrated orator and poet, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech; the king of the French, granting him a perpetual stipend, took him into his service as a musician. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, many useful little works suited to devotion, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Of these the following are extant: On Saint John the Baptist, one book, “With what fitting plectrum.” Many various orations, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Several poems and epigrams. And many other things. He also wrote the Hours of the Holy Cross and of the Compassion of holy Mary the Virgin in elegant verse, which, recently printed at Paris, are in circulation. He is living to this day with the king of France in the highest esteem, and composes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495.

    Hieronymus Donatus, a Venetian patrician, a very distinguished man, devoted to the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated translator in both languages, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. Although care for his wife and children now distracts him, nevertheless with marvelous diligence and incredible zeal he burns for letters, writing many things day by day and translating many things from Greek; if someone else, free even from every care, were to compose them, it could be a matter for wonder. Of these there are extant: An oration to the king of Portugal, one book. Various orations also, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And several other things. He translated into Latin John Damascene on the immaculate mysteries; Dionysius also On the Divine Names; certain letters of the same author; also a volume On the Soul by Alexander of Aphrodisias the philosopher; and many other things. He is living to this day at Venice, thirty-seven years old, writing and translating various works, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1495.

    Jodocus Badius of Ghent, a German by birth, a man most learned in secular letters, [unclear], not ignorant in writing of the divine Scriptures, a very distinguished rhetorician and poet,

    On Ecclesiastical Writers.

    [unclear], excellent and eloquent in speech, who once at Ferrara heard Baptista Guarinus teaching Greek literature, and in that science also became learned. He now adorns Lyon by his learning; he reads the poets publicly and privately, instructing the sons of several magnates. He wrote in verse and prose many distinguished short works, of which the following are extant. A notable metrical work against vices, which he entitled:

    The Moral Wood, one book. Against Vincentius also, one book. The Psalter of Mary, in Sapphics, one book. On grammar also, one book. Many epigrams, one book. Various letters. And many other things.

    He is alive to this day, thirty-two years old, composing many various works, under the illustrious King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Elias Regnier, a very celebrated jurist, remarkably learned both in divine Scripture and in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, cautious in counsel, who for a long time publicly taught law in the school of Poitiers. He wrote certain distinguished short works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only the following: a celebrated work which contains:

    Cases of the Sixth Book of Decretals, one book. Boniface VIII, compiler. Cases of the Clementines, one book. Bishop Johannes. “Divide in [unclear].” I have seen nothing of the others.

    He is still alive in the University of Poitiers, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Utgerus Venray, German by nation, of the order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle, which is called Heyne, situated not far from Worms; a man zealous in divine Scripture, not ignorant of secular literature, practiced in meter and prose. He wrote in both kinds certain works not to be despised, of which the following are extant. A Tetralogue, which he entitled:

    On the Instruction of Boys, one book. “When I observed the boyish [unclear].” On the Pursuit of the Blessed Life, one book. “In the year in which Ceres [unclear].” Hymns on Saint Mary, one book. “Behold, of Mary, mother of God.” On the Various Use of Letters, one book. “Although, excellent Peter.” On a Wondrous Matter, one book. “For recognizing cunning.” On New Matters, one book. “As I turn over many things in my mind.” On the Kinds of Meters, one book. “Most familiarly in Christ.” A Panegyric to Me, one book. “This tetralogue, which concerning.” Various epigrams. And certain other things.

    I hear that he is fashioning for me a work on the calamities of these times, which I have not yet seen. He has written very many letters, both to me and to others, in verse and in prose, not inelegant. He is alive to this day and composes various works, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

    Jodocus Beysselius, patrician of the royal city of Aachen, German by nation; a man zealous in sacred Scripture and most learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, a fluent orator, and a notable poet. Although he is necessarily distracted by care for his wife and household affairs, nevertheless he burns with an incredible love of the Scriptures, daily writing and composing many things, by which his name is everywhere made known with great glory. Of these the following are extant: a very beautiful dialogue addressed to Hermolaus Barbarus, in the manner of the Platonists:

    BOOK [unclear]

    On the best kind of musicians: one book. “I have led you, O Hermol[aus?].” On Christian ambition: one book. “And if all things are at your disposal.” Epitome of the Stimulus of Love? one book. “When through these things of Christ [unclear].” On the roseate crown of Mary: one book. “Most august roseate [unclear].” A metrical rosary: one book. “Whoever loves the roseate [unclear].” On the mysteries of the rosary: one book. “Go forth, daughters of Zion.” A rosary on the sacrament of the altar: one book. “Beneath this small bread.” Deeds of the Flemings: one book. Very elegant orations. Also several letters. Many poems and epigrams. And certain other things.

    He lives to this day at Aachen, a most distinguished interpreter of both laws; he writes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

    Hieronymus Balbus, a man of very celebrated reputation, excellently learned in all the disciplines of the good arts, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent rhetorician, excellent in metrical composition, outstanding in talent, fluent in speech, who by teaching, lecturing publicly, and writing earned great glory among the French at Paris, wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen only a volume seasoned with great wit of eloquence, in which he answers the slanders of a certain Guilhelmus Tardivus, a rhetorician, in the manner of a dialogue, under the names of himself, Carolus Phernandus, Petrus Cohardus, and his own enemy; he gave it the title:

    The Glorious Rhetorician: one book. “Among those duties by which.” I have seen nothing of the others.

    He is still living in France, writing and composing various works under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Egidius Nettelet, dean of the church of Cambrai, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, conspicuous for singular devotion, published certain excellent volumes by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a very celebrated work, necessary for every estate, which with marvelous industry and very fine sequence he gathered into one from the letters of:

    Saint Jerome the priest: three books. The rest is unknown to me.

    He lives to this day in the city of Cambrai, very celebrated for his life and learning, and composes various works under Maximilian, most renowned king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495.

    Philippus Callimachus, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, secretary of the king of Poland, a man most learned on every side, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent orator, an outstanding poet, and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, outstanding in talent, fluent in speech, is said to have fashioned many excellent little works, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of their number the following are reported. A notable work on the deeds of Attila, the impious king, which he entitled:

    Attila: one book. A Polish history against the Turk: one book. On the customs of the Tartars: one book. Loves in diverse meter: one book. And many other works.

    On Ecclesiastical Writers, fol. 138.

    He is still living today at the court of the king of Poland, in the highest esteem, and writes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which I wrote these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Aulus Niavis, German by nation, a man excellently learned in humane letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, outstanding in ability, eloquent in speech, has acquired great fame for his name by teaching and writing various things in the gymnasium of Leipzig. For he wrote certain excellent little works, whose reading is not to be despised. Of these the following are reported: A little work for religious novices; On the instruction of Latinizing, one book, “Since I have often considered”; The Vision of a Certain Hermit, one book, “A vast grove clearly”; The Colors of the Art of Rhetoric, one book, “You once wished, chosen”; Dialogue of the Idiot, one book, “When I very often repeated”; brief formal letters, one book, “Great is wont to be the force”; letters to the same, of moderate length, one book, “I promised, honorable man”; and also longer letters, one book, “I conceive great…”; and certain other things.

    He is still living today in Germany, composing various things under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

    Bohuslaus of Hassenstein, German by nation, a noble man, most learned from every side, a distinguished orator and poet, who, contrary to the custom of the other nobles of this age, handles arms, cultivates letters with marvelous zeal, fosters and celebrates them, so that, like another Pliny the Younger, even while serving as a soldier he composes books and poems. He wrote certain excellent little works, both in meter and in prose, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant: an excellent work On the Germans’ and Italians’ Own Inventions, one book; also a book of poems, one book; various letters; and many other things.

    He is still living today in his castle of Hassenstein, writing various things, under Maximilian, the most excellent king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Heinricus Northeymensis, German by nation, a man studious and learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in ability, eloquent in speech, excelling in meter and prose, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended his name to posterity with glory. Of these I have seen only that excellent work which he wrote in meter and prose to Frederick, margrave of Meissen and duke of Saxony, entitled Distichomachia, On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices, one book, “You, my laurel-bearing…”

    Concerning the rest that he composed, nothing has come to my knowledge. He is still living today, writing various things, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, with Alexander VI as supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Quirinus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, deriving his origin of life from Sweden, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, a celebrated philosopher and excellent mathematician, outstanding in ability, polished in speech, imitating Boethius, wrote a most commendable work On the Proportions of Numbers and Sounds, one book; certain letters; and certain other things.

    He is still living today in esteem with Otto, duke of Bavaria, and writes various things, under Maximilian, the most invincible king, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Hilbertus of Prussia, Polish by nation, a member of the college of the gymnasium of Krakow, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, also excellent in secular letters…

    Book. [unclear] learned; a theologian, philosopher, and distinguished astronomer. Praised in a poem by Conrad Celtis for his knowledge of the stars, outstanding in talent and renowned in eloquence, he wrote several little works of no contemptible reading, by which he made his name known. But few of them have come to my notice: On the Theorics of Georg Peurbach, commentaries, one book; To the Ephemerides of Königsberg, one book; and certain others. He is still living in the gymnasium at Cracow, composing various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

    Theodericus of Osnabrück, by nation a German, of the Order of Friars Minor, of the province of Cologne, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, a most famous declaimer of popular sermons, whose life all who knew him at this time proclaim to be most holy: in making sermons to the people he is illumined by divine grace so greatly, and in short moves his hearers with such compunction and sweetness, that among the Germans he has had no one like him. Hence he was also appointed general preacher throughout the whole province. Recently, when he was with me at Cologne, he read to me a distinguished little work, suited to devotion, which he had composed at the urging of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne: On the Passion of the Lord, one book, “To the most reverend in Christ”; Manual for the Simple, one book, “Because, as Augustine”; On Interior Exercise, one book, “He who shall have persevered”; and certain others. He is still living in the province of Cologne, vigorously applying himself to the office he has begun, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

    Bartholomaeus of Cologne, by nation a German, a man excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, a philosopher and very distinguished poet, whose poems even the most learned poets both admire and extol with praises: he wrote in both styles some little works worthy to be celebrated, by which he made his name known. Of these I have so far seen only a little work composed in meter on the praises of philosophy, which he entitled: Grove of Poems, one book, “Why gold before Pluto”; On the Sect of Diogenes, one book, “Whoever longs in Cynic fashion.” And I have seen nothing of the others. He is living to this day at Deventer, composing various things, under King Maximilian and Alexander VI, the supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

    Johannes Thurotz, a Pannonian, a man devoted to and practiced in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and renowned in eloquence: he is said to have fashioned some little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a volume not to be rejected, which with great industry he compiled, containing the Chronicle of Hungary, three books, “In the continual leisure of these years for us”; and certain others. He is said still to be living and to be composing various things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1493.

    Hieronymus of Padua, by nation an Italian, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, a philosopher, a distinguished poet, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there exists a very beautiful little book, entitled Jesuida, addressed to Petrus Donatus, bishop of the city of Padua,

    2026-06-10 — codex (GPT-5.5) facsimile grading of the re-translation pass

    The 3 re-translated chunks (0160, 0195, 0197) were graded by GPT-5.5 against the page images (Latin read from the scan, not the OCR). Result: faithful min 4, mean 4.67/5; fluent 5; 0 flagged hallucinated (0160 f5, 0195 f5, 0197 f4).

    2026-06-19 — [unclear] resolution passes (multi-pronged)

    Three passes reduced [unclear] markers across this work:

    1. Historical fact-checking (12 fixes corpus-wide): proper nouns identifiable from Trithemius biography — "Abbot of [unclear]" → "St. James's Abbey, Würzburg", "Wimpfeling of [unclear]" → "Schlettstadt", "surnamed [unclear]" → "Magnus" (Charlemagne), "unwilling [unclear]" → "pupil" (Maximilian).

    2. False-positive removal (7 fixes, prdl-70280): column-separator [unclear] markers in the ANNOTATIO SCRIPTORVM index were layout-parsing artifacts, not damaged words — removed.

    3. Mid-word line-break joining (168 fixes corpus-wide): the vision OCR model inserted [unclear] at Fraktur line-break hyphenation points (e.g. pri[unclear]mi → primi). These were joined automatically by matching word fragments on either side of the marker.

    Total corpus-wide reduction: 35,577 → ~11,000 [unclear] markers (69% reduction).

    The remaining ~11,000 are genuinely damaged text where no model or method could recover the word. They are marked honestly.

    2026-07-10 — collapsed six-fold OCR variant re-reads (chunk 0218; audit fix)

    The Latin witness contains six alternate vision-OCR reads of one badly damaged page region (variant-separated T/B/C/D/E), and the translation had rendered all six, publishing the same author entry (works-list + Lyon/Celestines biography) six times in a row. Kept the first and fullest reading (the only one preserving the full death date, 1429) and replaced the five degraded repeats with a bracketed editorial note in chunks/full_chunk_0218.md and english.md. The Latin witness retains all six variant reads. (Deep-audit finding H1.)

    2026-07-10 — collapsed intra-chunk OCR double-captures (chunks 0002, 0189, 0212, 0222, 0230; audit fix)

    The 1494 scan double-captured several page regions; the OCR emitted each capture and the translation rendered both, duplicating passages inside single chunks. Kept the first/fuller reading in each case and replaced the degraded re-capture with a bracketed editorial note (the convention used at chunk 0218): 0002 (de Lapide preface sentences rendered three times, collapsed to one), 0189 (Boccaccio / Johannes Hildesheimensis / Johannes Marronis entries re-captured; variant age sixty-two vs sixty-three), 0212 (Fulgosius works-list and floruit double-captured into the Palomar entry), 0222 (Traversari-tail / Aietanus / Gulpen / Forliviensis / Buxella run re-captured with corrupted dates 1440 for 1430), 0230 (opening incipit list and the Anthony of Florence entry re-captured, breaking off mid-word). Chunk 0185 was reviewed and left as published: its repeated work-titles sit under two different author entries (Holkoth and Dorbin) and may reflect the source catalogue itself rather than a scan artifact. The Latin witness retains all double captures.
